slide_text: The Neuroplasticity Theory Why some people always seem calm. @successoutright
Ever notice some people stay calm, even when things go wrong? **It's not personality, It's not luck.**
Scientists discovered something wild about our brain. It rewires itself based on what we repeat. **It's called neuroplasticity.**
Try brushing your teeth with your other hand. **It feels awkward.**
But do it for a few weeks. Your brain adapts. **It becomes automatic.**
And here's what most people miss: **Thoughts are practice too.**
Every time you repeat negative self-talk "I always mess up." "This always happens to me." **Your brain adapts.**
Over time when something goes wrong... **Negative thoughts appear instantly.** Almost automatic. Because you trained them
If you interrupt negative thoughts and practice kinder reframes **your brain starts learning a new path.**
Next time when a negative thought show up Pause. Reframe. **Choose a gentler default.**
Over time, you will notice the kinder thoughts always show up first. Without effort. **It becomes the new default.**
That's neuroplasticity in action. You didn't change your life. **You changed your defaults.** That's how a happier brain is built.

notes:
**Slides 2–10 are one repeated frame, deliberately.** Blurred still from the cover photo as background, a single blue folder icon, the skill name in plain sentence case, then one or two sentences. Nine slides, identical layout. There is no texture variation at all — the opposite of what the craft file demands — and it works *because the post is an inventory*. The repetition is the point: it reads as a folder you are scrolling through. Texture rules apply to arguments, not to lists.

**Every skill is named as a filename.** `Webinar-Deck`, `VSL-Script`, `Optimize-Ads`. Hyphenated, no spaces, no marketing name. That single choice does more to make the thing feel real and already-built than any claim in the caption.

**Each description answers "what does it do" and then "so what".** Two sentences maximum. The second sentence is always the reason to care — *"very little editing is needed before recording"*, *"the changes are automatically made for me"*, *"trained on over 10K+ direct response emails"*. Never a feature without its consequence.

**Proof is borrowed, specifically and by name.** Russell Brunson, Alex Hormozi, 10K+ direct response emails, 150-200 slides, 1 to 30 minutes. Numbers and names on almost every slide. This is the claim-proof law running at full strength across an entire post.

### The CTA — the part worth stealing

**The ask is on its own slide and nothing else is on it.** No summary, no recap, no second ask. One question, one instruction.

**The escalation is the whole trick:** *"Want Access To ALL These Skills?"* then, in smaller type underneath, *"(Plus 50+ others)"*. The post spent nine slides making nine things wanted, then reveals at the last possible moment that nine was a fraction. The reader's sense of what they are about to get jumps by 6× one line before they are asked to act.

**The grid of blank folders is the visual of the withheld thing.** Not a list, not a description — just identical unlabelled folders. It shows there is more without giving any of it away.

**"Comment 'SKILLS' + I'll send a link"** — the word is lifted from the cover slide, so it has been in the reader's head since the first frame. It is one syllable, impossible to misspell, and it is the literal name of the thing.

**The result: 2.1K comments against 518 likes.** People who would not spend a like *will* spend a comment when a comment is the price of the thing.

**What it gives away and what it holds back:** it names all nine skills and says exactly what each does — so it answers *what* completely. It never says how any of them were built, what is in a skill file, or how to make one. The *how* is entirely behind the word.

file: Library/Posts/08 - Claude Sucks at Design.md
title: Claude Sucks at Design
notes:
**The hook attacks the thing the audience loves.** *"CLAUDE SUCKS AT DESIGN."* Full stop, largest type on the slide. Every other post in this file opens with a promise; this one opens with an insult aimed at the tool the reader uses daily. It forces a reaction — agree and you need the fix, disagree and you have to swipe to argue.

**The resolution is one small line at the bottom: "These 42 skills fix it."** Tiny type inside a thin outlined box, dwarfed by the headline. The problem is shouted, the solution is whispered. That imbalance is what makes it a hook rather than an ad — you have to lean in for the second half.

**The design does what the post claims.** A carousel arguing that Claude produces generic design cannot itself look generic. It is styled as a 1970s technical spec sheet — registration marks, dimension lines, `SYSTEM.STATUS: ONLINE`, `BUILD: 2025.05.24`, `PRECISION: 8-BIT CLEAN`. **The format is the proof of the claim.** Compare the folder-icon slides in post 03: functional, forgettable, and fine there because that post's claim was about capability, not taste. Here the claim is about taste, so the artefact has to demonstrate it.

**42 items across 5 slides, and it never feels like a wall.** Because each slide is a *named layer* with its own count in the headline — 10 core, 8 creative, 10 system, 8 prompt, 6 security. The reader is never asked to hold 42 things, only "six layers". Numbering runs continuously 01–42 across slides, so the progress bar is built into the content.

**Every item is `slug-name` + a three-to-four-word gloss.** Never a sentence. `token-budgets: Context window token math`. The parallelism is absolute, which is what lets the eye scan forty-two rows without fatigue. Same filename-style naming as post 03 — hyphenated lowercase reads as *a real thing that exists on a disk*.

**Each slide ends on a bolded one-line summary** — *"Engineering flawless design output." / "Visual-first programmatic assets." / "Designing systems that respond."* A footer that tells you what the layer was *for*, after showing you what is in it. It converts a list into an argument.

| Slide ends | Next slide answers |
|---|---|
| "But folders alone won't work without this →" | The Schema File |
| "Now you need to feed it →" | Dump Everything |
| "Here's exactly what to say →" | Tell The AI To Build It |
| "Then the real power kicks in →" | Ask It Anything |
| "But who is this actually for? →" | This Works For Everyone |
| "One more thing to keep it clean →" | Monthly Health Check |
| "Save this before you forget it →" | The CTA |

Not one of them is a summary. Every one is **a question or a promise the reader now wants resolved**, and the next slide resolves it and opens the next. The chain is unbroken from slide 2 to slide 9. This is what "every slide creates a question, the next slide answers it" looks like when someone actually commits to it — and it is worth noting they *wrote the connective tissue out loud* rather than trusting the reader to feel it.

**The last one is the cleverest.** *"Save this before you forget it →"* is not a content promise at all — it is an instruction to save, disguised as a chain link, placed one slide before the ask. It boosts the save metric and delivers the reader to the CTA already in a compliant frame.

**The hook's power is subtraction.** *"It's not an app. It's not a plugin. It's just 3 folders on your computer."* Two negations then the reveal. The claim is not "this is powerful" but "this is smaller than you think" — **the NESB lever being pulled is Easy, hard, and nothing else.** The number 3 appears in the headline, in the folder graphic, and in the subhead.

**Slide 2 makes the whole system fit in three shell commands** and then says *"That's the entire architecture."* Showing the complete thing on the second slide is a risk that pays off — it proves the "just 3 folders" claim immediately, and the remaining six slides become about *making it work* rather than about what it is.

**Numbered steps 01–07 in the slide titles**, plus a square progress bar at the bottom of every slide that fills in as you swipe. The reader always knows how much is left. Compare post 08, which did the same job with a running 01–42 count.

**Slide 7 is the "who is this for" slide, placed second-to-last.** Four audiences, one line each, each written as the outcome *that* person wants. It is a widening move right before the ask — anyone who had not yet placed themselves in the post gets a chance to. Note the italic line above it: *"If you're consuming it, you should be compounding it."*

**The comment word is `'Brain'`** — rendered in a monospace code box with a cursor clicking it, matching the file-system aesthetic of the whole post. And the deliverable is named as three specific artefacts: *"Schema file. Folder structure. The exact prompt that builds it."* Not "a guide".

**It gives away almost everything and still asks.** The full CLAUDE.md schema, the build prompt, the audit prompt are all printed. Same finding as post 06 — what is sold is the copy-paste, not the knowledge.

slide_text: **3 Folders** *raw + wiki + outputs* **I Built My Second Brain With 3 Folders** It's not an app. It's not a plugin. It's just **3 folders** on your computer.

**01. Three Folders.** ``` $ mkdir raw/ $ mkdir wiki/ $ mkdir outputs/ ``` *That's the entire architecture.* - `raw/` — Your junk drawer of notes, highlights, and saved articles - `wiki/` — Where the AI writes clean, organized knowledge pages - `outputs/` — Answers and drafts the AI generates for you → **But folders alone won't work without this**

**02. The Schema File** Create one file called **CLAUDE.md** in your project root. It tells the AI **what your knowledge base is about** and how to organize it. > **# Knowledge Base Schema** > **## What This Is** > A personal knowledge base about [YOUR TOPIC]. > **## How It's Organized** > `raw/` contains unprocessed source material. Never modify these files. > `wiki/` contains the organized wiki. AI maintains this entirely. > `outputs/` contains generated reports, answers, and analyses. > **## Wiki Rules** > Every topic gets its own .md file in wiki/ > Every wiki file starts with a one-paragraph summary > Link related topics using [[topic-name]] format > Maintain an INDEX.md that lists every topic > When new raw sources are added, update wiki articles > **## My Interests** > [List 3-5 things you want this KB to focus on] → **Now you need to feed it**

**03. Dump Everything** 1. **Drop anything into raw/** — Bookmarks, screenshots, notes, transcripts 2. **Export notes from any app** — Apple Notes, Notion, Google Docs. All of it. > **Don't organize it. Don't rename files.** > **The AI's job is to sort the mess. Your job is to dump it.** → **Here's exactly what to say**

**04. Tell The AI To Build It** ``` Read everything in raw/. Compile a wiki following the rules in CLAUDE.md. ``` One prompt. Your entire knowledge base **organized.** → **Then the real power kicks in**

**05. Ask It Anything** - *"What are the gaps in my understanding of X?"* - *"Compare what source A says vs source B"* - *"Write me a briefing on X using only what's in here"* **ASK → SAVE → SMARTER** Every answer gets saved back into the wiki. The next question builds on the last. **That's the compounding loop.** → **But who is this actually for?**

**06. This Works For Everyone** - **Content Creators** — Which topics, hooks, and formats actually perform. Query your own data. - **Business Owners** — Every meeting, decision, and client detail. One place, forever searchable. - **Researchers** — 50 papers synthesized into one wiki. Ask questions across all of them at once. - **Students** — Build the wiki a textbook never gave you. Personalized, connected, yours. → **One more thing to keep it clean**

**07. Monthly Health Check** **Scan wiki → Flag errors → Auto-fix** > THE PROMPT > *"Review the entire wiki. Flag contradictions. Find unsourced claims. List dead ends. Fix what you can. Flag the rest."* Once a month, run one prompt. The AI audits everything. **Contradictions, unsourced claims, dead ends.** It fixes what it can. Flags the rest. → **Save this before you forget it**

file: Library/Posts/10 - The 6 Golden Exercises.md
title: The 6 Golden Exercises
notes:
**The hook works by pre-empting the objection in the subhead.** *"Not because they're the 'best.'"* The scare quotes around *best* kill the argument the fitness audience always starts. Then the actual reason lands: *because together they cover everything.* **Answering the objection on slide 1 rather than slide 2** — worth contrasting with post 04, which saved each objection for the following slide. Both work; the difference is that here the objection would have stopped the swipe.

**Slide 2 exists only to justify the number.** *"Why 6, not 50 exercises"* — it defends the constraint before teaching anything. The number in the headline is the promise (Easy: only six things), so the number is what has to survive scrutiny first.

**Every exercise gets the same second bullet, and it is the best writing in the post:** *"The movement behind every chair you get out of." "Every bag, box and child you pick up." "Shopping, luggage, a child on one hip."* The abstract pattern is translated into a domestic moment the reader had this week. **Loads → the anatomy. The movement behind → the life.** Muscle names alone would be a textbook; the second bullet is what makes it a reason to care.

**One real citation, in tiny print, once.** Bull et al., WHO Guidelines, with a DOI. It is not shouted and it is not repeated. Its presence on the one slide that makes the load-bearing claim is enough to colour the whole carousel as sourced.

**No CTA at all.** No comment word, no "follow for more", no offer. The last slide is just the sixth exercise. The only persistent element is the MD credential in the footer of every slide. This is the counter-example to posts 03–09: a post that harvests authority and saves rather than leads. Worth noting because it is a deliberate choice, not an omission — the account is a doctor's brand where the credibility *is* the funnel.

**The illustration style is the credibility.** Clinical greyscale anatomy with the working muscles highlighted in red, on white. It looks like a medical reference, not a fitness post, which is the same principle as post 08: **the visual register is an argument about who is talking.**

slide_text: HOW TO GET PEOPLE *addicted* to your storytelling

THERE ARE **6 LEVELS** OF STORYTELLING *Ladder with the levels listed:* 6. The Maestro · 5. The Translator · 4. The Architect · 3. The Champion · 2. The Illusionist · 1. The Reporter The higher you climb, the more *addictive* it gets.

LEVEL 1: STORYTELLING *The Reporter* The reporter includes the core facts of the story but sequences them in a super predictable way. *A retro TV reading:* This happened. then this happened. then this happened. Level 1 is like newscaster reading off a teleprompter. It's informative but not that engaging. Graduate from this level as soon as possible.

LEVEL 2: STORYTELLING *The Illusionist* You have the facts. Now add hooks that pull people in. Great hooks don't change the story. They redirect attention. *Diagram:* AUDIENCE EXPECTATION line crossed by an arrow at STORY PIVOT, pointing to MISDIRECTION. Make them expect one thing… then take them in a different direction. Do it a few times, and you've got their attention.

LEVEL 3: STORYTELLING *The Champion* Keep the facts + hooks. Now add stakes. Show the problems, use cases, or characters that make people feel connected to the story. Without stakes, the story falls flat. No stakes = no emotional connection.
LEVEL 4: STORYTELLING *The Architect* Now we're entering advanced storytelling. Keep the facts, hooks, and stakes then add arcs and loops. Loops are mini-subplots that open, build tension, and close.

LEVEL 5: STORYTELLING *The Translator* Take everything from the first 4 levels then add clarity + comprehension. Make sure your message is 100% clear. Reframe the message. Use better visuals. Add that final layer of polish. That's what takes good storytelling to the next level.

LEVEL 6: STORYTELLING *The Maestro* This level is about adding your unique fingerprint. Your style. Your voice. Your way of telling stories. *A head made of a fingerprint.* You won't have it figured out at first. But over time, you develop it and it becomes the layer that sets you apart.

file: Library/Posts/11 - Two Birthday Cakes.md
title: Two Birthday Cakes
notes:
**The cover is an image, not a claim.** *"I watched a woman buy TWO birthday cakes for herself."* No lesson, no promise, no number-of-things. It works because the picture is odd enough to need explaining — and the subhead tells you the explanation exists and is being withheld: *"And then she told the cashier why."* **One concrete strange fact plus the promise of the reason.**

**Eight slides of story, one slide of meaning.** The lesson does not appear until slide 8, and even then it is one sentence. Slides 2–7 contain no advice whatsoever. This is the exact inverse of a bad story carousel, where every slide stops to explain itself. **The meaning is earned by withholding it.**

**Real dialogue does the heavy lifting.** *"Two birthdays?"* — *"No. They're both for me."* — *"I finally realized I don't have to keep treating myself the way other people treated me."* Three quotes across nine slides, each on its own slide, each highlighted. Nothing the writer says in their own voice is as strong as any of these. **Quote the person; don't paraphrase them.**

**Every slide has a big line and a small line, and they do different jobs.** The big serif line is the event. The small line underneath is the narrator's private reaction — *"I thought maybe it was for her grandkids…"*, *"And for some reason, I immediately started listening."*, *"And honestly… I felt something shift in my own heart."* The reader gets the scene and the guide's reaction to the scene simultaneously. That second voice is what makes it feel like being told something rather than being shown something.

**The narrator is a witness, not a hero.** They do nothing in the story except stand in a queue. Every good thing belongs to the woman. Compare with the arrogance problem: **the writer's role is to have noticed, not to have done.**

**Slide 3 plants a wrong guess and slide 4 corrects it.** *"I thought maybe it was for her grandkids… But her answer surprised me."* → *"No. They're both for me."* The narrator makes the same assumption the reader is making, out loud, and is wrong in the same way. That is the cheapest and most reliable curiosity device in the whole file, and it costs one line.

**The pivot from her to you happens only on the last slide.** Eight slides about a stranger, then *"maybe there's a younger version of you"*. No "can you relate?", no "tag someone". The turn is late, short, and direct.

**Delayed keyword payoff.** The final line — *"HAPPY BIRTHDAY TO YOU"* — recontextualises the whole post as a card written to the reader. The cover was about a stranger's cake; the last line makes it the reader's birthday.

**No CTA of any kind.** Like post 10, it monetises nothing directly. This is a save-and-share/emotional-reach post. Worth knowing the shape exists, but it is not the shape for a lead-gen carousel — the lesson to take is the *storytelling*, not the ending.

---

slide_text: **I watched a woman buy TWO birthday cakes for herself.**
**I was behind her in line at the grocery store.** She had a few normal things on the belt… and **two** little birthday cakes.
**The cashier smiled and asked,** **"Two birthdays?"** I thought maybe it was for her grandkids… *But her answer surprised me.*
**She kind of laughed, looked at the cashier, and said,** **"No. They're both for me."** And for some reason, I immediately started listening.
**Then she told the cashier her story.** She grew up in a home where birthdays **weren't really a thing**. No cake. No candles. No waking up feeling special.
**So every year now, she buys *two cakes*.** ♥ **One** for the woman she became. ♥ **And one** for the little girl who deserved to be celebrated all along.

**Then she said something I haven't stopped thinking about:** **"I finally realized I don't have to keep treating myself the way *other people treated me*."** And honestly… I felt something shift in my own heart in that moment.
**It reminded me that healing isn't always some huge, dramatic moment.** Sometimes it *looks* like buying the cake.
And maybe there's a younger version of you who still needs to hear: **You mattered then. You matter now. And it's not too late to celebrate that *you're here*.** HAPPY BIRTHDAY TO YOU. ♥

It can understand a "formula" to structure it's writing to match how you write, but it always misses the mark slightly. When you write your own content, script and captions, even if it's not "optimized", there is a **sprinkle of authenticity** that AI cannot replicate – and thats the **imperfectness** of you.

SKILL I'M KEEPING FOR MYSELF: **pen and paper for ideation** I've tried brainstorming with AI for ideas for content and business and I started to realize 2 things: 1. The ideas weren't that great or generic 2. It made me feel dumber and lose my creativity When I started going back to writing down my ideas, even if it was messy, all over the place, and made no sense, **I always had better ideas.** I could also feel my brain working harder as I was trying to go deeper on my own thoughts. AI is good for general research, **but it is not creative or unique.**

SKILL I'M KEEPING FOR MYSELF: **responding to emails and DMs** Many high performers will say this is a waste of time, but I disagree. Whenever I get a DM from a follower or an email from a customer, I do not use AI. **I want my personality to come through.** I want my customer to feel like "wow, this brand actually cares". Or when a follower asks me a question, I want them to know it's actually me talking to them. **Human connection over automation.**

SKILL I'M KEEPING FOR MYSELF: **deep learning via primary sources** Alot of people use AI for research, and I think it's good for initial research, but it can also leave out **valuable sources.** Now with **AEO** (agentic engine optimization), you can easily "hack" your way into being a source that AI references, even if it's not a credible source. AI can give you general research about a topic, but often times it's just a summary about a topic. If you truly want to go deep into a topic, I find using sources like PubMed, Google Scholar, physical books, even YouTube, is going to **help you learn better.**

SKILL I'M KEEPING FOR MYSELF: **discernment and decision making** Never outsource your decision making to a robot, or to someone else. Even if your decision isn't the "right one", at least you will have come to that decision yourself, and **you can learn from the decision.** I used to always ask other people for their opinions, and it can cloud your judgement and **weaken your decision making skills.** You need to learn how to trust your gut, backed with data, and then make a decision based on that. You can get AI to help with drafting out pros and cons that you might not have considered, but **never let it decide the final choice.**

SKILL I'M OFFLOADING TO AI: **transcribing** Instead of typing, I mostly transcribe via WisprFlow (which is technically an AI tool). It does not alter anything I say, it simply transcribes word for word what I say into my online databases like Notion, Google Docs, Notes, emails, and even text messages. I communicate best via speaking out loud. By using a transcription tool, it allows me to get my **most raw thoughts** down **without any editing or filtering** compared to when I write. Even if it's messy, the sentences and tone of voice are **the most unique and creative.**

SKILL I'M OFFLOADING TO AI: **formatting documents** After brainstorming my ideas and transferring it to my digital spaces, I find using AI for organizing information, formatting documents, and creating templates is extremely helpful. This is a task I've never enjoyed doing and found as a waste of time. I know some people love making pretty templates, but not me. This is a "skill" I'm willing to offload to AI to save time, because it can actually **do a better job than me**, do it faster, and takes away a task that I actually dread so I can focus on doing what I do best: **ideation and execution.** This is admin busy work that AI should handle.

SKILL I'M OFFLOADING TO AI: **synthesizing information** AI does a great job of summarizing information from books, scripts, documents, and publications. However, I think it's important to **actually read** through these mediums on your own first, but it can be helpful to get AI to help you synthesize key learnings after you've done the work. Think of this like a **second round of learning**, where AI can help remind you of the key points, or even pull out insights that you may have missed or forgotten about. Whenever I've read a book vs. getting AI to just summarize the book, I learn and absorb the info from **first hand reading** way better.

SKILL I'M OFFLOADING TO AI: **reporting and analytics** I will always use AI to pull data and analytics for social media, Shopify, Klaviyo, etc. However, I will always review the raw numbers first, and then have **AI act as a second pair of eyes for what I might be missing.** I don't want to lose the skill of **understanding how metrics and numbers work.** But I also want to make sure I'm not missing any key insights (which is where AI can help). AI can also be helpful in helping me understand metrics, especially if I've never learned them before.

with AI increasingly dominating our world, way of life and work, it's extremely important to be a conscious AI user. If you offload every skill and task to AI, you are no longer learning or using your brain. "Use it or lose it" is very real when it comes to cognitive function.

file: Library/Posts/111 - If We Ran a Design School.md
title: If We Ran a Design School
notes:
**The cover is a thought experiment.** "If we ran a design school, this is what we'd teach" makes the reader the student and the author the dean. It sets a bar ("what's missing from every school") that every month on the map has to beat.

**The roadmap is drawn as a route, not listed.** A yellow dashed line winds across the slides from Month 1 to Month 10 on a blue grid like a blueprint. Swiping follows the line, which is the closest a carousel gets to a journey, and each month is a headline plus two or three lines in small type.

**Each month names the thing other schools skip.** "Most people start with tutorials. We'd start here." / "Every designer will touch this in 2026. Zero schools are teaching it properly yet." / "This gets zero time in most curriculums." The comparison is the argument, and it repeats in different words so the reader keeps score.

**The close is one sentence with a symmetry.** "Most design education teaches tools. We'd teach thinking. The tools change. The thinking doesn't." The final ask is the three platform icons, Like, Save, Share, with no comment word. Compare [[98 - How to Build a Design System]] and [[67 - How Minimalist Design Takes More Work]] for other design posts.
cover_head: If we ran a design school, this is what we'd teach 2–6 — the roadmap
cover_sub: (one yellow dashed line on blue grid paper joins the months) Month 1 Principles before tools. Hierarchy, contrast, alignment, spacing. The things that don't change no matter what replaces Figma in 5 years. Most people start with tutorials. We'd start here. Month 2 Typography and colour as communication. Why this typeface feels safe. Why this red creates urgency. Not decoration. Tools. You can't make the right decision until you understand what each one is saying. Month 3 Systems thinking. Designing one screen is easy. Designing 40 connected screens where every decision affects the next one that's the actual job. This is where most designers plateau. Month 4 AI fluency. The one missing from every curriculum right now. Not how to use AI tools. How to design around them. Conversational UI. Generative interfaces. What to do when the output isn't fixed it's probabilistic. Every designer will touch this in 2026. Zero schools are teaching it properly yet. Month 5 Strategy before execution. What is the actual problem? Who has it? What does success look like? Figma opens last. Not first. Month 6 Content design. Words are design decisions. The error message. The empty state. The onboarding headline. Most schools give this to someone else. We wouldn't. The designer who controls both the layout and the language is twice as hard to replace. Month 7 Data literacy. A/B results. Heatmaps. Drop-off rates. Not to become an analyst to never be overruled in a meeting again. The designer who brings a heatmap to a decision conversation is unkillable. Month 8 Presenting and defending your decisions. The designer who can't explain their choices is always vulnerable. The one who can always wins the room. This gets zero time in most curriculums. Month 9 Building in public. The designers winning in 2026 aren't the ones with the best portfolios. They're the ones people already know. Documenting and sharing your work is a career skill. It compounds forever. Month 10 The business of design. Pricing. Positioning. Getting clients. Keeping them. The stuff no design school teaches and the stuff that actually determines your career trajectory.

file: Library/Posts/112 - The Art of Worrying Less.md
title: The Art of Worrying Less
notes:
**The cover gives three verbs.** "Stop overthinking, trust yourself, and find peace in the present." The reader knows what they will get and the three promises map onto the six points that follow: overthinking (1 and 5), trust (2 and 3), present (4 and 6).

**Each point is a heading and four short paragraphs, nothing else.** There are no images, no icons and no colour but the lime highlight on the heading. At about 45 words a slide it is the most text-led post in the file, and it stays readable because every paragraph is one or two sentences and the headings can be read alone.

**The lines are plain and gentle, never urgent.** "That is okay." "Let them." "Allow yourself to figure things out slowly." The post reads like advice a friend gives in the evening, which is why it suits a book-themed account and gets saved.

**It ends on a quote and four words.** The Mark Twain line, "I have had many troubles in my life, most of which never happened", is the whole argument of the post in one sentence, and "That's it." closes it. There is no CTA slide. Compare [[71 - The Art of Taking Nothing Personally]] from the same account.
cover_head: ==The Art of Worrying Less== How to stop overthinking, trust yourself, and find peace in the present.
cover: ==The Art of Worrying Less== How to stop overthinking, trust yourself, and find peace in the present.
cover_lines: How to stop overthinking, trust yourself, and find peace in the present.
cta_text: ==6. Life Will Always Have Uncertainty== You will never know exactly how everything will turn out. And that is okay. You do not need to know the entire path. You only need to take the next step. As Mark Twain wrote, **"I have had many troubles in my life, most of which never happened."** Do not spend today worrying about a tomorrow that may never come. That's it.

slide_text: ==The Art of Worrying Less== How to stop overthinking, trust yourself, and find peace in the present.

==1. Most Things Are Not As Bad As You Imagine== Your mind can turn a small problem into a hundred possible outcomes. You imagine what could go wrong, what people might think, and what might happen next. But most of those things never happen. Do not let an imagined future disturb your present peace.

==2. You Do Not Need To Have Everything Figured Out== It is normal to be uncertain about what comes next. You do not need to know exactly where your life is going. Sometimes clarity comes after you take the next step. Allow yourself to figure things out slowly.

==3. Deal With Problems When They Actually Happen== You do not need to solve tomorrow's problems today. Some things will resolve themselves. Some things will become clearer with time. And some things simply are not worth worrying about. Trust yourself enough to handle life as it comes. If something happens, you will deal with it then.

==4. Focus On What You Can Control== You cannot control what other people think. You cannot control what has already happened. You cannot control everything that happens tomorrow. But you can control how you respond today. That is where your peace begins.

==5. Not Every Thought Deserves Your Attention== Just because a thought enters your mind does not mean it is true. Your mind will sometimes create fears, doubts, and worst-case scenarios. You do not have to believe everything you think. Some thoughts are meant to pass. Let them.
==6. Life Will Always Have Uncertainty== You will never know exactly how everything will turn out. And that is okay. You do not need to know the entire path. You only need to take the next step.
As Mark Twain wrote, **"I have had many troubles in my life, most of which never happened."** Do not spend today worrying about a tomorrow that may never come. That's it.

title: You're Looking for Content Ideas in the Wrong Place
notes:
**The cover says the answer is not where the reader thinks, and then says "Let me explain...".** The three lines together are a contract: a claim, a teaser, a promise to go slowly. The reader who has run out of ideas knows exactly which place they have been looking.

**The first body slide names the mistake with a picture of it.** "Most 9-5ers build content backwards. They open Instagram, look at what everyone else is posting, then ask: 'What should I talk about?'" gives the reader's own habit in the second person, in the order they do it. "That's because you're just searching outside yourself" is the diagnosis.

**Each slide is a bold headline on the left and the body on the right.** Two columns of small light type on a dark photo, with bold used for the one sentence per slide that carries the idea ("Perspective is rare", "The experience belongs to you. The lesson should belong to them.", "Repetition builds recognition."). It is the densest slide format in the file after the book-page posts.

**The three questions in slide 3 are the method.** "What did I believe 3 years ago that I disagree with now? What lesson took me way too long to learn? What advice would I give my younger self?" The reader can use them the same night, so the post delivers before the ask.

**The CTA is a new video lesson.** "Comment 'BASE' and I'll send my brand new video lesson revealing how to build a personal brand from scratch that actually stands out." The word is a base, the thing the post told the reader to build from. Compare [[88 - The One Line That Makes Me $200,000 a Month]] and [[41 - How To Know What Content To Make]] for the same topic.

slide_text: You're looking for content ideas in the wrong place. (And it's probably not where you think.) Let me explain... *Photo of a man at two monitors in a dim room, a lamp glowing. Footer on every slide 2–7:* YOU'RE LOOKING FOR CONTENT IDEAS IN THE WRONG PLACE · page number 02–07

Most 9-5ers build content backwards. They open Instagram, look at what everyone else is posting, then ask: "What should I talk about?" So eventually everything starts sounding the same. That's because you're just searching outside yourself before looking at what you already know. Here's what I mean by that...

Topics are everywhere. **Perspective is rare.** You can make another post about productivity, career growth, leadership, or personal branding... But what makes someone remember you is what your experiences taught you about those topics. Ask yourself: → What did I believe 3 years ago that I disagree with now? → What lesson took me way too long to learn? → What advice would I give my younger self? Those answers are harder to copy. That's the beginning of you actually standing out.

Your story alone isn't valuable to your audience. What they can take from it is. Instead of: "Here's something that happened to me." Think: "Here's what happened to me, what it taught me that could help you." **The experience belongs to you. The lesson should belong to them.** That's why strong personal brands can tell the same stories repeatedly without becoming repetitive. The story stays similar, but the lesson changes.

If all you do is teach information people can Google, you become easy to replace. Your audience also needs to know: • what you believe • what you disagree with • what you would do differently • what you think people misunderstand • what standards you refuse to lower You don't need controversial opinions just to get attention. **You need clear opinions that reveal how you think.** Information makes you useful. A point of view makes you memorable.

You don't need a brand new idea every day. **Your comments, DMs, saves, shares, and conversations are already telling you what deserves more attention.** If people keep responding to the same: problem, story, belief, question, or desired outcome... *that's a signal.* Strong creators don't abandon a message because they already posted about it once. They find new ways to say what their audience clearly needs to hear again. **Repetition builds recognition.** *Screenshot of insights:* Interactions 147,442 · Followers 19.4% · Non-followers 80.6%
💬 Comment "BASE" and I'll send my brand new video lesson revealing how to build a personal brand from scratch that actually stands out.

file: Library/Posts/114 - How I Make a Stupid Amount of Money With a Blank Note.md
title: How I Make a Stupid Amount of Money With a Blank Note
notes:
**The cover gives the method as a habit, not a promise.** "Any time I want to make a stupid amount of money, I open a blank note in my phone" sells a repeatable action the reader can do in the next minute, and the empty Notes window on the photo is the proof it is that small. The word "stupid" does the work a big number would do elsewhere.

**Every claim is followed by a screenshot of the note.** The slide says "get technical" and the next picture shows a goal written with a figure and a finish line. The reader never has to imagine what the instruction looks like. The same note frame repeats on six slides, so the repetition reads as a template they can copy.

**Slide 11 admits the boring part before the reader has to.** "This is where giant goals get REALLY boring. Which is great" plus "(this is also where most people give up, btw)" names the point the reader is most likely to quit, then turns it into the reason the method works.

**The CTA is a follow request, not a comment word.** It lists the author's four themes ("business identity, neuroscience, faith, money, habits") and ends on a threat of a missing feed. Compare [[113 - You're Looking for Content Ideas in the Wrong Place]] and [[88 - The One Line That Makes Me $200,000 a Month]], which both use a comment word instead.

slide_text: any time I want to make a *stupid* amount of money, I open a blank note in my phone...
and this can apply to ANY BIG GOAL you have, btw...not just fitness.
i don't start with motivation and I definitely don't wait until i "feel ready." *i open my notes app.* (the first step will always be easy to do, but that's why not everyone will do it)

first, i write the exact goal. not "make more money." not "get healthier." **the number. get TECHNICAL.** i want to weigh 140 lbs. i want to run 3 miles. i want to make $100,000 in a month. *Screenshot of a note:* THE GOAL: Make $100,000 in one month. Not "have a good month." Not "make more money." $100,000 collected revenue. I want to know EXACTLY when I've hit it.
you *don't* become a different person and THEN start acting differently. you act differently long enough that eventually... **you become a different person.**

same with fitness. *not* ~~"lose weight."~~ more like... *Screenshot of a note:* FITNESS GOAL: Lose 30 lbs. Get to 140 lbs. Fit comfortably into a size 4/6. Feel STRONG, not just smaller. Have good energy. Maintain it without spending the next 5 years losing and gaining the same 20–30 lbs.

and with money, i pick the EXACT number. (usually one that feels JUST out of reach.) then i write what hitting that number would tangibly change. *Screenshot of a note:* $100K MONTH. What would this actually change? More money invested in real estate. More money invested in my family. More money given away to ____. More help outsourced to buy time back. More incredible experiences with my family. More freedom to make decisions based on what I WANT instead of what something costs.

and i make those things measurable enough that **i can't lie to myself.** *Screenshot of a note:* TODAY: Did I post? Did I make the offer? Did I follow up? Did I work out? Did I eat according to the goal? Did I keep the promises I made to myself? YES or NO.

then i reverse engineer the note. if THAT is where i want to end up... what needs to happen this month? this week? and eventually: what do i need to do *today?* *Screenshot of a note:* OK SO HOW DO I ACTUALLY GET THERE? $100,000 this month = $25,000/week. What would need to happen every week? What needs to happen every day? What are the 3–5 actions that ACTUALLY create revenue? What offers am I selling and how many units? Everything else is secondary.

when i **quit drinking**, the note wasn't just "stop drinking." i wrote what i wanted my actual life to feel like without it. *Screenshot of a note:* WHY I'M QUITTING DRINKING: I want clear-headed Saturday mornings. I want to be fully present every single day. I want to stop waking up with that looming guilty feeling of "did I do anything wrong." I want to be able to feel uncomfortable emotions without numbing something to change how I feel. I want to get closer to God and be able to listen and hear His voice clearly. I want to feel FREE.

this is where giant goals get *REALLY boring.* which is great. because i stop trying to "change my whole life" and just focus on the handful of things i need to repeat. (this is also where most people give up, btw.) *Screenshot of a note:* THE BORING PART. Do the daily stuff. Then do it again tomorrow. Then again. Stop needing every day to feel exciting. The giant goal is made up of a stupid amount of very normal days.

and if the plan isn't working, i change the HOW before i decide the goal is impossible. change the route, keep the destination the same. **there are always like 9,000 ways to get anywhere you're trying to go.**

if you're into the intersection of business identity, neuroscience, faith, money, habits, and PRACTICAL tips to become the version of yourself you need to be to achieve the things you want... you're gonna like it here.

one of the most important skills you can learn in life ...is to shoot your shot. There's a specific kind of person who ends up with the best opportunities, the best friendships, the career that looks like luck from the outside. It's never the most qualified person in the room. **It's the one who's willing to look a little delusional.** *A film still of a man in a suit with the caption:* you are absolutely capable of creating the life you can't stop thinking about

here's what people get wrong about shooting your shot They think it's about confidence. It's not. It's meant to feel scary and uncomfortable. At least a couple of times a week, I email or DM people I admire — professionally or personally. There's no reason for me to think this will work, but I do it anyway. You know what they say...closed mouths don't get fed.

**01. pick your goals** know what you're aiming for before reaching out. • **get specific.** A job you want, a room you want in, a friend group, a skill you want to learn, or just more clarity on what your next step is. • **keep the list short.** Choose 2–3 goals you want to work on right now to avoid analysis paralysis. • **some examples:** creating a network in a new industry, understanding how someone made a career pivot, landing a role at a specific company, getting feedback.

**02. choose your people** divide them into three categories: • **peers.** People in the same realm as you, doing similar work, at a similar stage. • **mentors or clients.** More senior people a few steps ahead who could be the key to unlocking your next opportunity. • **big shots.** The names that feel slightly delusional. Worth adding to your list even if the odds are lower. LinkedIn is the best place to find the right people.

**03. shoot the shot** • **be thoughtful.** No AI slop or generic emails allowed! A well-crafted, thoughtful message is so much more likely to get a reply. • **make one clear ask.** Don't bury it in context. Be clear and specific about what you want. • **follow up.** Most people are busy. Follow up twice in two weeks, and after that, graciously let it be. *Photo of a woman in a blazer holding a phone, a sticker reading* I don't want a mediocre life sorry

here's a little example Hi [Name], I'm [your name]. I'm currently [what you're doing]. I've been following your work for a while and just wanted to say I really love [specific thing about their work], especially [something even more specific, a project, a decision, a piece of writing]. It's a genuine source of inspiration. I'll be honest, I feel a little nervous writing this! But here's what I'm hoping for: [your ask, one sentence] Would you be up for a quick coffee chat sometime? Or if easier, I can send over my questions via email. Totally get it if you're slammed — I want to be respectful of your time! Thanks so much, either way! [Your name] *A red margin note:* we love a vulnerable diva

the worst thing that can happen is they say no or (more likely) you never hear back. And sure, rejection sucks. It hurts and feels embarrassing. But I can almost promise you you'll be over it by next week. But the upside is huge — the amount of work, the opportunities, some of my closest friends — all came from doing things that had no business working out. **If you actually do this — write the list of dream people, dream opportunities, dream collaborators, and send the messages — your life looks completely different in six months.**

now go shoot all your shots and watch the magic happen. *Red background. A still of a man in sunglasses with the caption:* I love the hustle. I love the game. I love coming from nothing. I love the uncertainty. I love the feeling of knowing it's a matter of time.

file: Library/Posts/12 - If Claude Writes Your Content.md
title: If Claude Writes Your Content
notes:
**The hook is a question the reader cannot answer.** *"If Claude writes your content, why on earth would I wire you $18k to access your thinking?"* It is aimed directly at the reader's business model, uses a specific dollar figure, and has no comfortable answer. Notice it is framed from the *buyer's* side — "why would **I** wire **you**" — so the reader is forced to stand where their own client stands.

**Slide 4 is the concession slide and it is load-bearing.** *"By the way: I LOVE AI."* Placed early, in the largest type, unqualified. Without it, everything after slide 3 reads as an anti-AI rant and half the audience leaves. With it, the argument becomes *"I use this daily and here is where it breaks"*, which is much harder to dismiss. **When you attack something the audience uses, concede your own use of it before you press the attack.**

**The argument descends one layer at a time, and each slide is one link.**

> everyone uses AI (2) → I can spot it in 30 seconds (3) → but I love AI (4) → not for creative work (5) → because it kills self-trust (6) → so your 10/10 becomes a 6/10 (7) → so she *processes* instead of *experiences* (8) → which matters at high ticket (9) → because she's buying your brain, not information (10) → and I know you meant well (11) → but the opposite is happening (12)

No slide skips a rung and no slide carries two. **Twelve slides is only tolerable because each one is a single move.**

**`processes` vs `experiences` is the whole post in two words.** One italicised word against another. That contrast is set up on slide 8, justified on 9–10, and paid off in the last line of slide 12 — *"buys from the person she can actually experience."* **A carousel this long needs one two-word distinction that the reader can carry out with them.**

**It ends on the diagnosis, not on advice.** There is no "so here's what to do", no comment word, no offer. The last slide describes the reader's current situation and stops. For a consultant selling high-ticket thinking, leaving the reader with an unresolved problem *is* the sales mechanism — the missing step is the call.

**Slide 11 does the empathy turn immediately before the wound.** *"I love you because the fact that you're using AI for content tells me you care."* After nine slides of criticism, one slide of genuine credit, then the closing blow. Placing the kindness *second to last* is what stops the whole thing reading as contempt.

**The voice is unpolished on purpose, and the post is about exactly that.** Typos left in — *"doest"*, *"sububconsciously"*, lowercase *"i totally get that!"* — alongside swearing and quadruple exclamation marks. A carousel arguing that AI sands off "the little imperfections & rawness of your actual voice" would be self-refuting if it were clean. Same principle as post 08: **the artefact has to demonstrate its own claim.**

**Typographic restraint carries the seriousness.** Brown leather texture, one elegant serif, italics as the only emphasis, a small brand mark top and bottom. No arrows, no highlights, no screenshots. The look says "an essay", which is what it is.

**The two-tier text pattern is used on almost every slide**: a large serif assertion, a rule, then small-set explanation underneath. The big line is the claim; the small line is the reasoning. A reader can swipe the whole post reading only the big lines and still get the argument — which is exactly how carousels are actually read.

file: Library/Posts/13 - The Entire Industry Has Lost Its Mind.md
title: The Entire Industry Has Lost Its Mind
notes:
**The hook is a timestamp and a reaction, not a claim.** *"This morning I opened my IG explore page and I'm in shock."* It reports something that happened hours ago to a thing the reader also opens daily. **A dated personal observation makes an opinion feel like reporting.**

**Slide 2 is the evidence, and it is three real quotes.** *"Reels are dead, yapping is in"*, *"Claude just killed Canva"*, *"this is the next big thing and if you miss it your business is done"*. Not a paraphrase of what the industry says — the actual sentences, in quotation marks. The reader recognises all three because they scrolled past them this week. **Quote the enemy verbatim and you never have to argue that the enemy exists.**

**Slide 4 names the emotion under the behaviour.** *"And underneath all of it is the same rooted feeling: Fear."* Everything before it is symptom; this is the diagnosis. It is also the only one-word italicised noun in the post. This is the why-chain landing: not "people chase trends" but "people are afraid of being last".

**The turn is on slide 6 and it is a group, not an instruction.** *"Meanwhile there's a much smaller group of people who aren't playing that game at all."* The reader is not told what to do — they are shown a room they could be standing in instead. **Offering membership beats offering advice.**

**Slide 7 lists what the alternative is made of, in fragments.** *"Lived experience. Storytelling. Values you had way before you had a business."* This is the one place the staccato fragment style is used, and it works because it is a list of abstractions being pinned down quickly, not a story being told. Then it resolves into a full sentence — *"Connection people feel because they recognize themselves in you."*

**It closes on a statement of certainty, not a CTA.** *"Here's what I know for sure."* After 7 slides of criticism, an authority stake. And the final clause is the sharpest thing in the post: *"nobody has ever built a category defining brand by chasing whatever was 'working' that week."*

**Eight slides, one sentence each, no headings, no bullets, no images.** The entire design is a serif on brown leather. When the writing is this quotable, the design's only job is to get out of the way — and the identical framing across all eight slides makes the post read like pages of one letter rather than eight separate points.

**Same as post 12: no CTA.** Two posts from this account, neither with an ask. The pattern for this brand is *the argument is the advertisement* — anyone who agrees hard enough will go and find the consulting page themselves.

Every other hook is "Reels are dead, yapping is in" or "Claude just killed Canva" or "this is the next big thing and if you miss it your business is done"
The whole online business and coaching world is in a constant state of debate about the format, the trend, the algorithm shift nobody can actually prove is happening.
And underneath all of it is the same rooted feeling: *Fear*. What if we miss the next big thing‼ What if everyone else figures it out before we do!
So everyone stays trend focused. Chasing whatever someone screenshotted from a guru's post last week and is now selling back to their audience as the *'secret'* nobody else knows.

Meanwhile there's a much smaller group of people who aren't playing that game at all. They're not asking what's about to blow up. They're building something that was *never* designed to depend on a trend in the first place.

They're focused on what actually holds a brand together. Lived experience. Storytelling. Values you had way before you had a business. *Connection* people feel because they recognize themselves in you.

Here's what I know for sure. Trends will keep coming and cycling. The platform will keep shifting what it rewards. But *nobody* has ever built a category defining brand by chasing whatever was 'working' that week.

file: Library/Posts/14 - Pattern Behind Every Viral Reel.md
title: Pattern Behind Every Viral Reel
notes:
**The cover promises ten and the post delivers three.** The subhead says *"Here Are The 10 Things They All Have"*; only "the final three" ever appear. Whether that is a deliberate tease or a broken post, the effect on a reader is the same — **a headline number the body does not honour is the fastest way to lose trust**, and it is the clearest counter-example in this file to the numbered-list posts that do pay off (03, 08, 09, 10).

**Slide 2 is a well-built promise slide even so.** Assumption → correction → escalation → hook: *"think viral reels are random"* / *"but there's a pattern"* / *"Not one element. Ten."* / *"Once you see the pattern, you can't unsee it."* Four beats in four short lines. The two-word fragment *"Not one element. Ten."* is the strongest thing in the post.

**"Once you see it, you can't unsee it"** is a reusable curiosity device — it promises a permanent change in perception rather than a piece of information, which is a bigger claim at the same cost.

**The CTA is the weakest in the file.** *"Comment 🎬 if you want more posts like this."* No deliverable, no name, no reason. Compare posts 03/08/09: comment a word, get a specific named artefact. This asks the reader to do work for the account's benefit and offers nothing back — which is why it is worth keeping as a negative example.

**The cover image is unrelated to the content.** A swimwear photo on a post about reel structure. It buys the stop and then contributes nothing to the argument. Contrast post 08, where the cover art *was* the argument.

file: Library/Posts/15 - Claude Carousel Blueprint.md
title: Claude Carousel Blueprint
notes:
**Its structural model, stated outright on slide 5:** hook → problem → value that builds → insight that feels earned → natural CTA. That is the same spine as posts 04, 07 and 09, written down. Note it assumes a 12-slide carousel; the system's 4–9 range compresses the "Slide 3–8 value" band, not the shape.

**"Likes are fleeting. Saves are commitments."** The clearest one-line statement in the file of why a carousel is built differently from a reel — and a useful reframe for the goal: a save is a viewer telling you they intend to come back.

**"Saves happen when insights are earned, not delivered."** The strongest idea in the post, and it corroborates what post 11 does in practice: the meaning has to arrive after the work, not instead of it.

**It puts the big insight in the middle, not the end** — *"Not the beginning. Not the end. The middle where everything clicks."* Worth holding against post 01, where the pivot ("Thoughts are practice too") lands on slide 6 of 12 — exactly halfway. Two independent sources for the same placement.

**"Short sentences early. Longer paragraphs when they're invested."** A pacing rule with a reason: the reader's tolerance for text grows as they invest swipes. It explains why front-loading dense copy kills a post and why slide 7 can be twice the length of slide 2.

**Its own CTA contradicts its own advice.** Slide 8 says *"The final slide isn't 'follow me' or 'comment below'"* — and slide 10 is *"Comment ⭐ if you want more Claude tips like this!"*, a generic comment-below with no deliverable. Same weakness as post 14 from the same account. **The account can articulate the principle and does not apply it**, which is a useful reminder that a post explaining best practice is not evidence the practice was followed.

**Slide 9 is a checklist recap, and it earns its place** by converting the six preceding slides into four questions the reader can actually apply. A recap that reformats rather than repeats.

**Formatting habit worth stealing:** every teaching slide's title is a two-part line — italic serif clause in orange (*"Claude defines the"*) followed by bold sans in white (**"save worthy insight"**). Two typefaces, two colours, one sentence. It makes six differently-worded titles feel like one series.

file: Library/Posts/16 - Your Carousel Is Dying On The Cover Slide.md
title: Your Carousel Is Dying On The Cover Slide
notes:
**It uses its own cover as the ✅ example on slide 2.** The reader is looking at proof they already responded to — they swiped, so the good example is self-evidently good. Cheapest possible credibility.

**Every rule is a paired image, not a description.** ❌ on the left, ✅ on the right, black cross and green tick. No slide asks the reader to imagine what a bad cover looks like. **Show the failure and the fix side by side rather than describing either.**

**"One is information. One is a promise."** The single most useful line in the file for step 4. *"Here are some tips"* versus *"Stop using Pinterest. Here's why"* — and it maps exactly onto the system's two shapes. Their "promise" is the Promise shape; their "revelation" cover (from post 15) is the Starter shape.

**"They swipe to solve a problem or satisfy curiosity. Your cover needs to do one of those two things."** A cleaner binary than the five-rule checklist the system currently uses — worth testing as a first-pass filter on any headline set.

**The 0.5-second test is more aggressive than the system's current standard.** *"Can someone read your cover in 0.5 seconds while scrolling at full speed? If no, make it bigger. If still no, make it bolder."* Note the fix offered is typographic, not editorial — they assume the words are fine and the size is wrong.

**Slide 7 is the reframe, and it lands late on purpose.** *"They design the carousel. Then they design a cover to match it. That's backwards. The cover should drive the carousel. Not follow it."* This directly contradicts the system's step 8 instruction to **write slide 1 last**. Worth holding both: the system's reasoning is that you cannot promise value you have not built; theirs is that a cover written to fit finished content will always be a description rather than a hook. The resolution is probably that the *idea* of the cover must lead, and its *wording* is finalised last.

**Slide 8 is a five-box pre-publish gate** — the same device as the system's own pre-delivery gate, reduced to five questions and one instruction: *"If any answer is no, redesign. That's it."*

**"Not generic stock photos that look like everyone else's."** Their own covers use styled editorial photography of people mid-gesture, consistently. Note this is the same account whose post 14 used an unrelated swimwear photo — the rule is stated better than it is followed.

You have 2 seconds to convince them to swipe. Most covers try to do too much. Explain everything. Set expectations. Be clever. **Your cover's only job: create curiosity.** The brain stops scrolling when there's a question to answer. A cover that creates intrigue gets the swipe.

If it's small, it fails. If it's hard to read, it fails. If it requires thinking, it fails. **Can someone read your cover in 0.5 seconds while scrolling at full speed?** If no, make it bigger. If still no, make it bolder. **Friction kills engagement. Clarity breeds clicks.**

| Bad cover | Good cover | |---|---| | "Here are some tips" | "Stop using Pinterest. Here's why" | **One is information. One is a promise.** People don't swipe for information. They swipe to solve a problem or satisfy curiosity. **Your cover needs to do one of those two things.** Benefit-driven hooks speak to the person's immediate need, not the carousel's topic.

Color contrast. Text contrast. Visual contrast. If your cover blends into the feed, it disappears. If your cover stands out, it stops the scroll. **The feed is visual noise. High contrast cuts through it.**

✅ One message. One visual direction. One promise. ❌ Not five things competing for attention. ❌ Not generic stock photos that look like everyone else's. ❌ Not a design that contradicts your brand voice. **Your cover should feel like it belongs to you. Not borrowed from someone else.**
**They design the carousel. Then they design a cover to match it. That's backwards.** The cover should drive the carousel. Not follow it.

☐ Does this make someone want to swipe? ☐ Can someone read it in half a second? ☐ Is the benefit immediately clear? ☐ Does it stand out from the feed? ☐ Does it feel like my brand? If any answer is no, redesign. That's it.

file: Library/Posts/19 - The Claude Workflow For Carousels That Sticks.md
title: The Claude Workflow For Carousels That Sticks
notes:
**Slide 2 is a diagnostic hook, and it is the best opener shape in the file for a professional audience.** It does not make a claim; it tells the reader to go and check their own data. *"Count how many got saved more than 50 times. Count how many drove DMs. Count how many people actually remembered a week later."* Three counts, escalating from a platform metric to a human one. Then the verdict: *"If the numbers are low, you've been treating Claude like a caption generator."*

**The reader convicts themselves.** They cannot argue with numbers they just looked up. Compare the [[13 - The Entire Industry Has Lost Its Mind|post 13]] hook — also an observation, but of someone else's feed. This one is of the reader's own.

### The four things it says to feed in before writing — all of which the vault already half-has

1. **Three past high-performing posts.** This is exactly `Successful Posts/DNA.md`. Confirmation the folder is the right idea.
2. **A list of banned AI words.** *Unlock, Tapestry, Leverage, Delve.* The vault has a kill list in the Headline Brain but no equivalent for slide copy. **This is a real gap.**
3. **A specific sentence-length rhythm.** Not "be conversational" — a measured rhythm. The vault says "write it as it would be said out loud", which is vaguer than this.
4. **A style guide, not an adjective.** *"We don't just say 'be funny.'"*

### The Hook Architect — a method the vault does not have

> *Identify the most common advice in the niche, then write 5 hooks that argue the opposite.*

This is a generative procedure for contrarian headlines, and it is more mechanical than the why-chain. The why-chain finds the *emotion* under a question; this finds the *received wisdom* to invert. They are complementary: the why-chain tells you what they are afraid of, this tells you what they have already been told a thousand times. **Together they are the gap sentence.**

Note it also asks for the audience's *"biggest hidden frustration"* — the thing they cannot say out loud, which the why-chain is designed to reach.

### Narrative arcing — three fixed temperature points

**Slide 1 High Tension → Slide 5 "Aha!" → Slide 9 Bridge to Action.**

Third independent confirmation of mid-post insight placement (see [[15 - Claude Carousel Blueprint|15]] and [[01 - The Neuroplasticity Theory|01]]). For a 4–9 slide carousel the equivalent is roughly: tension on 1, aha at the midpoint, bridge on the last.

**"Write like a screenwriter, not a marketer."** One instruction that would have prevented the copywriter-staccato failure already logged in `Carousel Craft`. A screenwriter writes what a person would say; a marketer writes fragments for emphasis.

### Visual friction — a genuinely new idea

> *"If the text is 'Simple,' the image should be 'Complex.'"*

The image should **contrast** with the text rather than illustrate it. Most of the weak posts in this file illustrate (post 14's swimwear photo illustrates nothing at all); the strong ones contrast — [[08 - Claude Sucks at Design|post 08]]'s furious voxel creature against a clean typographic claim, [[11 - Two Birthday Cakes|post 11]]'s delicate line-drawn cake against a story about childhood neglect.

### The Human Pass — a self-audit the vault should adopt

> *"What part of this sounds like a robot wrote it? Where am I being too formal?"*

And the advanced move: **rewrite the conclusion three times — as a Mentor, as a Peer, as a Skeptic — and pick the one that sounds most like you.** That is a concrete way to hand a voice decision back to the client instead of guessing it, which is exactly the writer/author split the vault is built on.

**Slide 8 closes on a question, not an instruction.** *"Are you using Claude to think, or just to type?"* It reframes the entire post as a standard rather than a workflow, and it is the line a reader would repeat.

file: Library/Posts/20 - Hacks I'd Gatekeep If I Wanted ADHD Entrepreneurs To Fail.md
title: Hacks I'd Gatekeep If I Wanted ADHD Entrepreneurs To Fail
notes:
**The hook is the strongest structural device in this file.** *"Hacks I'd gatekeep if I wanted ADHD entrepreneurs to fail."*

It is a **negative-frame list**. Instead of "8 hacks for ADHD entrepreneurs" — which is information, and would be skipped — it implies (a) these are good enough that withholding them would be sabotage, (b) other people *are* withholding them, and (c) the writer is choosing not to. Three claims in one sentence, none of them stated.

**It converts a generic listicle into a generous act.** This is the single most transferable line-shape in the file, and it works for any list:

> *"Things I'd keep quiet about if I wanted [audience] to stay stuck."*

**The audience is named in the hook.** *"ADHD entrepreneurs"* — so the filtering happens on slide 1 without narrowing the topic. Anyone with ADHD who runs anything stops. This is exactly the vault's own principle: keep the topic wide, narrow in the wording, not the subject.

**Every hack has a name and a mechanism.** *"magic 5 to-do list"* is a name you can repeat; the body says exactly what to do and what you get — *"6 tasks done in 30 minutes plus dopamine to kick start your day."* Naming a tactic makes it feel like a possession rather than advice.

**The reason is always ADHD-specific.** *"Less tools to manage = less executive funtion."* / *"ADHD brains justify perfecitonism as productivity in the last 20%."* The same eight hacks written for a general audience would be a generic productivity list. **The mechanism is what makes a common tactic feel written for one person.**

**One photograph on all ten slides, with the headline repeated small at the bottom of every slide.** Zero design cost, and the repeated headline means any single slide screenshot carries the hook. Note this is the Inventory pattern again — total layout repetition across a parallel set.

**Typos left in** — *perfecitonism*, *funtion* — as in [[12 - If Claude Writes Your Content|post 12]]. On an ADHD account this reads as consistent rather than careless.

**The last slide is an introduction, not an ask.** *"Hi I'm Ari, I help ADHD entrepreneurs build businesses that work with their brains."* The reader has just received eight useful things and only then finds out who was talking. The bracketed *"[and i'm really f***ing good at it]"* is the whole voice in one line — the claim would be arrogant in plain type, and the brackets make it a joke that still lands as a credential.

**The CTA is a follow, and it is written in the reader's language:** *"hit follow to build TF out of your ADHD owned business."* Weaker than a comment-word funnel for lead capture, but consistent with a personal-brand account.

file: Library/Posts/21 - 8 Things I've Learned In A Healthy ADHD-ADHD Relationship.md
title: 8 Things I've Learned In A Healthy ADHD-ADHD Relationship
notes:
**The headline is a list of eight, but every item is a confession.** *"We don't keep score because we both forget the score."* That is not advice — it is an admission of a shared deficit reframed as an accidental advantage. The whole post runs on that move: take the thing the audience is ashamed of, and show it working.

**Each item is a claim in the title and a personal cost in the body.** *"[1] We don't keep score…"* then *"In the past, people were always bringing up the things I did wrong 3 months ago… I felt at a severe disadvantage because I couldn't even remember 3 days ago."* The title is the payoff; the body is the wound it healed. **The reader has to feel the old pain to value the new state.**

**Nothing here is general.** *"We joke that we're 2 gremlins amongst humans."* / *"the same level of tolerance for disorganization."* No item would survive being rewritten for a general audience — which is precisely why they land. Compare with the failure mode in `Carousel Craft`: generic slides are what happens when the specific was never asked for.

**The staccato problem is absent because these are spoken sentences.** *"Literally everywhere we go, we're the ones having the MOST fun and joy."* Long, slightly run-on, capitalised for emphasis mid-sentence. It reads as someone talking, not as copy being emphasised — the distinction the vault has been trying to name.

**One photo, all nine slides, headline in the same position.** Identical to post 20's construction. This account's entire visual system is *one good photograph plus text*, and it costs nothing to produce. Worth noting against the assumption that carousels need design.

**The CTA asks for the reader's version, not for a keyword.** *"If you're in an ADHD-ADHD relationship I wanna hear your learnings too!! Drop it in the comments."* No deliverable and no capture — but unlike the weak *"comment if you want more"* CTAs in posts 14/15/17, this one gives the reader something to actually say. **An invitation to contribute beats an invitation to request.** It will produce a comment section full of stories, which is its own reach engine.

**Signed by both of them.** *"♡ Ari + Chirs"* — handwritten, at the end. It turns the post from content into a note.

file: Library/Posts/22 - Why Doing Everything Right Makes You Forgettable.md
title: Why Doing Everything Right Makes You Forgettable
notes:
**The hook is a paradox stated flatly.** *"Why Doing Everything Right Makes You Forgettable."* No number, no audience label, no promise of a method. It works because it accuses the reader of a virtue — the thing they are proudest of is the thing being blamed. Note the eyebrow (`BRANDING FRAMEWORK`) and the footer (`WHY WE LOVE THE BRANDS WE LOVE`) do the audience-targeting that the headline refuses to do, so the headline stays clean.

**Slide 2 states the question the post exists to answer, and says so.** *"Which raises the question this post is about."* Explicit, unembarrassed. Then the question itself is genuinely hard: *"What makes one touchpoint capable of that when the twenty next to it are not?"* **Naming the question on slide 2 sets the contract** — everything after is measured against whether it answers this.

**"Everything in your business is decent. That is the problem."** Two sentences, the second reversing the first. This is the same construction as [[10 - The 6 Golden Exercises|post 10]]'s *"Not because they're the 'best.'"* — take the reader's assumed compliment and make it the diagnosis.

**"Extraordinary is not a better version of decent."** The line the whole post turns on, and it is a *category* claim rather than a *degree* claim. The diagram makes it visual before the sentence lands: six identical squares, then one diamond. Not a bigger square.

**Slide 4 supplies the mechanism, and this is what separates it from an opinion post.** *"Memory does not record what it predicted."* Then the consequence in three escalating clauses: *"nothing happened. The customer is not unimpressed. They are unaware."* The middle clause pre-empts the obvious misreading and the third replaces it with something worse. **Correcting the reader's likely paraphrase mid-sentence is a very high-level move.**

**"They are unaware"** is the whole insight in three words — worse than disliked, because there is nothing to fix.

**The diagrams are drawn, not decorative.** Dots draining out of circles across four "ON TIME" deliveries into `NOTHING RECORDED`. Same placement as [[09 - I Built My Second Brain With 3 Folders|post 09]]'s "this works for everyone" slide: broaden on the penultimate beat so nobody excludes themselves right before the CTA.

file: Library/Posts/30 - Your Attention Span Is Fcked.md
title: Your Attention Span Is Fcked
notes:
**Sixteen slides survive because each one is a single sentence and a drawing.** Almost no slide carries more than about twenty words. The vault's 4–9 range assumes slides of paragraph density; this post proves the ceiling is set by **words per slide**, not slide count. A 16-slide post that reads in forty seconds is shorter than a 6-slide post of dense copy.

**The three-tier text pattern is used consistently:** small grey lead-in, large black claim, small grey elaboration. *"You trained it into this." / **"So train it back"** /* — and slide 15 drops the third tier entirely for emphasis. **Varying which tiers are present, while keeping the same grid, is how it gets texture without changing layout.**

**Slides 2–4 build the mechanism as a three-beat causal chain, one beat per slide.** Boredom appeared → you reached → relief arrived in one second. Then the line that closes it: *"Your nervous system wrote that down."* The reader is never blamed; the nervous system is the actor. **Externalising the fault is what keeps a diagnosis post from feeling like an attack.**

**"And relief came in one second flat"** — a specific duration where "quickly" would do. Same instinct as the numbers in the inventory posts, applied to a feeling.

**The prescription slides give physical, checkable instructions.** *"Twenty pages, a walk without headphones, work in a single tab."* Not "practise deep focus". Three concrete objects. Compare [[10 - The 6 Golden Exercises|post 10]]'s *"every bag, box and child you pick up"* — both translate an abstraction into things the reader can picture in their own week.

**Slide 14 is the honesty slide and it is the reason the post is credible.** *"The first two weeks will suck. Withdrawal always does…"* Naming the cost before the reader discovers it is what separates advice from a pitch. Then it resolves into the most precise image in the post: *"one day a book holds you for an hour and you realize the baseline is moving back."*

**"You trained it into this. So train it back."** The whole argument in eight words, placed on the second-to-last slide, in the largest type. Same paired-verdict shape as [[26 - This Is How You Build An Irresistible Brand|post 26]] and [[22 - Why Doing Everything Right Makes You Forgettable|post 22]] — **the strongest line gets its own near-final slide, alone.**

**The hook uses the audience's own register.** *"f*cked"* with the asterisk, then *"here's how to fix it →"* in plain lowercase. The profanity buys the stop; the lowercase second line makes the promise feel casual rather than salesy.

**One illustration style throughout — pencil sketch on white.** Sixteen different drawings, one visual grammar. It is the cheapest possible way to give every slide a distinct image while keeping the post unmistakably one object. Note the drawings are always *the noun of the slide* (a hand, a phone, a pill, a seedling, a pencil), never decoration.

**The CTA is a newsletter, and it is weak by this file's standards.** *"Get my daily field notes of what I'm building, breaking, shipping… (link in bio)."* Off-platform, no comment word, and the three bullets describe the author's activity rather than the reader's benefit.
