file: Library/Posts/55 - How To Waste Your Marketing Budget.md
title: How To Waste Your Marketing Budget
notes:
**The cover hijacks the promise of an easy improvement guide.** “how to waste your marketing budget / in 6 easy steps” puts a desirable instructional shape around an undesirable result. “easy” suggests these errors require little effort and may already be happening. The reader is invited to recognise waste, not merely consume another list of ways to optimise spending.

**Slide 2 punctures apparent abundance with a tiny actual change.** “make 30 versions of the same ad” initially sounds like energetic testing; “change three words in the hook” shows how little changed. That numerical mismatch does the accusation more precisely than “your ads lack variety.” “Meta is gonna LOVE all these exciting choices!!!” then overperforms enthusiasm so the reader hears the author's disbelief in the label “creative diversification.”

**The next mistake moves from the advertiser's activity to the customer's interrupted intention.** “send every click to the homepage” follows an ad-production error with the destination of the traffic it produces. “one specific product/offer” establishes a clear reason for clicking before “start their journey over from the beginning.” The sarcastic “naturally” asks the reader to hear how unnatural the instruction is; the wink keeps the criticism conversational without undoing it.

**The first question pair imitates the speed of an anxious operator.** “campaign had a weird morning? REBUILD IT” → “new ad hasn't converted after eleven minutes? KILL IT ASAP!” makes an observation instantly become a drastic command. “weird morning” and the absurdly exact “eleven minutes” expose the thin evidence. After the homepage problem, this slide shifts to the advertiser's handling of results, showing another way effort can destroy rather than improve a campaign.

**The vague-copy example lets the reader discover the missing product.** “‘elevate your everyday.’ beautiful. what are we selling? who knows <3” follows the loud intervention slide with a soft, polished line that says almost nothing. “beautiful” grants the aesthetic appeal for one beat before the blunt commercial question removes it. The affection symbol makes the failure sound charmingly indefensible, which is the joke: pleasant language has concealed the absence of an offer.

**The discount question chain ends in the consequence hidden inside the supposed fix.** “sales are down? 20% OFF!!! still down? 30% OFF!!!” repeats the intervention rhythm of slide 4, now escalating the size of the concession. “eventually you can run a GOING OUT OF BIZ sale” is the darkest payoff: the seller's last sale becomes the destination of discounting as the automatic answer. The insight lands inside the example rather than in a separate warning about margins.

**The final practice names the surrender of judgment behind the other fixes.** “they MUST know something you don’t” makes assumed competitor authority explicit. “no need to investigate whether it’s actually working for them...” then leaves the omitted investigation hanging. After tiny ad variants, restless changes and automatic discounts, this last item broadens the problem from bad tactics to decisions made without evidence; it is a fitting endpoint even though the six items are not a strict sequence of prerequisites.

**The CTA finally gives a sincere instruction, then makes the inversion explicit.** “follow us for daily marketing and ecomm advice :)” is the first plainly useful imperative after six destructive ones. “(just don’t do any of these things)” resolves the joke and prevents the advice voice from remaining ambiguous. The follow is earned by the specificity of the diagnoses, rather than by a promised resource the slides have not demonstrated.

**This is a satirical Inventory, with a small argument inside each item.** “make your ads incredibly vague” is deliberately bad advice; “what are we selling?” supplies the test that defeats it. There is no single late revelation and no master question chain across all six mistakes. Each heading is prosecuted by its own miniature scene, with “LOVE,” “REBUILD,” “KILL” and “OFF” letting the reader hear the overconfidence that causes the waste.

file: Library/Posts/56 - You’ve Been Brainwashed If You Think.md
title: You’ve Been Brainwashed If You Think
notes:
**The hook accuses the reader of an influence before naming the influenced belief.** “sorry to break it to you but / you’ve been brainwashed if you think...” combines the social softener with an unusually severe word. “if” and the unfinished clause make the accusation conditional: the reader has to swipe to find out whether it applies. The attack is on what feels necessary or normal, not simply on how much someone spends.

**Slide 2 supplies a familiar calendar rule as the first test.** “you have to buy new clothes for each new season” completes the suspended cover sentence. “have to” is the pressure point; the claim is not that new clothes are inherently wrong. Beginning with seasonal shopping gives “brainwashed” an everyday referent before slide 3's “£250 a month” brings a sharper financial threshold into the argument.

**The recurring clause makes separate purchases look like one learned compulsion.** “you’ve been brainwashed if you think” returns before a gym, a holiday haul, bodycare and trainers. There are no literal questions, but every return asks the reader to test another belief against the same diagnosis. The repeated “need” moves the examples out of taste and into imagined obligation, which is how the list builds an argument rather than remaining a miscellany of expensive things.

**The middle examples identify replacement before exhaustion as the distortion.** “new products before finishing the ones you have” follows “a haul for your holiday” by challenging accumulation that does not even need an occasion. “multiple pairs of trainers for a hobby” then questions whether equipment has outgrown the activity it serves. “before finishing” and “for a hobby” give the criticism concrete limits; neither line requires the reader to reject all bodycare or exercise purchases.

**The sequence shifts from buying objects to obeying an audience.** “you need to hop on every trend” moves beyond a category of goods, then “you’re always expected to have your nails done” names social expectation directly. “always” makes the maintenance endless. Following this with “outfits aren’t meant to be repeated” reveals the same rule applied to clothes already owned: the pressure can devalue possessions without any change in their usefulness.

**The aesthetic line makes identity itself part of the shopping constraint.** “you need to choose and stick to an aesthetic” comes after the outfit-repetition rule, when the reader has already seen appearance become an obligation. “choose and stick” is a paired demand: first classify yourself, then remain consistent. The post broadens from isolated purchases to the idea that a person's everyday self must fit a stable, consumable category.

**The penultimate item changes direction to protect the reader's agency.** “doing your part doesn’t make a difference” breaks the run of beliefs about needing to buy. After being told that many wants are implanted, the reader could conclude individual choices are pointless; this line names that resignation as another distortion. It prepares the last imperative by making resistance feel consequential rather than merely frugal.

**The last line finally names the source and gives the reader a boundary.** “don’t let social media warp your normal” follows ten examples instead of preceding them, so “normal” now has specific content: seasons, monthly fees, unused products, outfits and aesthetics. “warp” carries the force of “brainwashed” without repeating the accusation. This is a behavioural CTA, with no follow, comment or product request; the earned action is to resist the standard the examples have exposed.

**This is an Inventory used as an Argument about manufactured necessity.** “it’s normal to buy” and “you’re always expected” reveal why the items belong together: the reader has mistaken a feed's repeated displays for rules of ordinary life. The main insight is stated most completely at the end, in “your normal.” The deliberately recurring prefix gives the reader ten chances to recognise one particular kind of pressure before that compression lands.

file: Library/Posts/57 - How You're Gonna Lock In For The Rest Of The Year.md
title: How You're Gonna Lock In For The Rest Of The Year
notes:
**The cover addresses a reader who wants a recovery, not merely a routine.** "How you’re gonna lock in for the rest of the year" supplies a remaining window of time, while "and pull that comeback" assumes a disappointing stretch came before it. "Gonna" makes the promise sound like a friend's confident instruction. "No gatekeeping" and "my full guide" then promise access to the practical means, giving the ambition somewhere to go.

**Slide 2 deliberately shrinks the scale of the promised comeback.** "Most people quit because they set the bar way too high on day one" follows a cover loaded with urgency. It explains why answering that urgency with a huge effort would fail. "One commit or ten pages a day" makes the correction tangible; "And never miss twice" introduces a recovery rule so a single bad day cannot disqualify the reader from the comeback.

**The goal slide replaces a finish-line question with an identity question.** "Forget the goal" follows "Start small," pushing beyond merely reducing the size of a target. "Who you want to be in 2027" gives the small actions a direction without demanding a result before the year ends. "So the new year isn't another fresh start" is the sting: the reader's appealing annual reset is recast as evidence that the previous attempt never became a way of living.

**The phone slide supplies the missing time after supplying the intended person.** "Your phone is where the day goes" comes after deciding who to become. The sentence treats wasted time as a place the reader already knows, not a moral failure. "Once scrolling takes effort" identifies the intervention: make the competing habit harder. "You can put it into the habits from the last slide" closes the causal loop between attention recovered and the identity just chosen.

**The physical advice lowers the author's authority just as it broadens the demands.** "I'm lacking here myself, so this one's for me as well" appears when the post adds exercise, food, and sleep to the reader's obligations. "Just look at my numbers lol" repeats that admission rather than pretending a perfect routine has been achieved. The cycle sentence then gives the item a reason to belong: changing one behaviour affects the others, so the body is part of the proposed comeback rather than a separate fitness topic.

**The reflection slide returns to the opening rule against doing too much.** "Pick one small thing to do better next week" follows the cycle of sleep, training, and eating, which might otherwise suggest fixing all three immediately. "Don't try to change everything at once" repeats the concern about the high bar on day one at a later point where overload is now more plausible. The main insight is cumulative: an identity changes through small repeated actions, then through small corrections to those actions.

**The tool claims work because personal language keeps interrupting the resource lists.** "My go-to blocker is Opal, but anything works" specifies what the author uses and immediately removes dependence on that brand. "I do mine in Notion and Claude" later makes the software part of an existing Sunday habit. The closing "I haven't organized it manually in months" gives automation a particular job: reduce the upkeep of reflection, so tracking does not become another reason to quit.

**The guide CTA has been seeded through conspicuously unfinished lists.** "+5 more suggestions!" in slide 2 and "+5 more free ones" in slide 3 promise additional material while giving useful examples on the slide itself. After habits, resources, a blocker, training tools, and a reflection method, "Comment ‘GUIDE’" refers back to the cover's "my full guide." The reader has evidence of what that guide will contain, although the final frame leaves the delivery mechanism unstated.

**This is a Build with resource curation inside it.** "Start small" → "Forget the goal" → "Put the phone down" → "Train your body" → "Reflect Weekly" assembles a way to sustain the comeback, rather than five independent productivity tricks. There is no literal sequence of questions; the implied questions move from how to begin, to what to aim at, to where the time comes from, to what supports the work, to how to keep improving. The books and apps answer those questions alongside the instructions.

file: Library/Posts/58 - I Say Let Me Get Back To You Instead Of Answering On The Spot.md
title: I Say Let Me Get Back To You Instead Of Answering On The Spot
notes:
**The supplied cover gives the reader a sentence to borrow before naming a philosophy.** "i say \"let me get back to you\" instead of answering on the spot" attacks the reflex to agree while somebody is waiting. The qualification "it buys me time to think, check my calendar" makes delay sound competent rather than evasive. The first payoff is immediately usable language, not a promise to become better at boundaries later.

**Slide 2 turns self-protection from a conversational skill into an administrative habit.** "i check my payslip every single month" follows a decision about how to answer other people with a decision about what to verify for yourself. "deductions, allowances, overtime" gives three places to look before "they rarely work in your favor" names the cost of trusting the system. The reader is invited to inspect something concrete rather than merely distrust an employer.

**The coffee item removes the awkward label before offering the career benefit.** "not networking-networking. just knowing people in other departments" follows the payslip check, moving from protecting current income to hearing about future openings. Repeating "networking" turns the intimidating professional performance into a recognisable exaggeration. "Before they're posted" then gives the casual coffee a reason beyond being sociable: access to information that is not public yet.

**The leave item refuses to let career protection become another form of overwork.** "i use all my leave credits" comes after cultivating contacts, a habit that could sound like extra work in spare time. "every single one" closes the loophole of using only a respectable portion. "nobody gets a trophy for unused vacation days" removes an imagined reward; "burnout doesn't care how loyal you were" removes an imagined protection. The two clauses dismantle both reasons a reader might keep sacrificing rest.

**The CTA makes saving the post an answer to bad advice.** "save this for the next time someone tells you to \"just work hard\"" appears in image 05, after four examples, rather than at the end of the supplied sequence. It finally names the idea those examples oppose: effort alone is sufficient career insurance. The save request is earned by an exact future situation in which the reader might need a counterargument. The subsequent "follow for more work related content" is broader and less tightly justified than that first request.

**The resume and brag document form the clearest local cause-and-solution pair.** "i won't remember my wins later" in image 06 creates the memory problem that "5 minutes, 3 bullet points" in image 07 solves. "what i did, what it fixed, who noticed" progresses from activity to effect to evidence of recognition. The final "what i did in march" makes the consequence of postponing the task sound like an actual appraisal conversation, not an abstract warning to document achievements.

**The first-person present tense makes each habit a reported practice rather than an order.** "i update my resume every 6 months, even when i'm happy" describes a precaution that does not depend on dissatisfaction. "not because i'm leaving. because" supplies the objection and correction in two clipped beats. The repeated "i" lets a reader test the author's reasons without being scolded; the time intervals make those reasons feel attached to an ongoing working life.

**The broad insight is distributed across the supplied late headline and final line.** "7 unsexy habits that protect my career in corporate" in image 08 names the collection after most of its evidence has appeared; "after 9 yrs" adds the duration of practice. The final "information is leverage" then explains why taking recruiter calls "even when i'm not looking" belongs beside payslip checks and records of wins. Protection means knowing what is owed, what is available, and what one's work is worth before a crisis forces the question.

**This is an Inventory with an argument against loyalty as insurance.** "even when i'm happy" and "even when i'm not looking" both detach preparation from an intention to leave. The seven habits cover agreements, pay, contacts, rest, records, and market knowledge; they are not sequential steps or episodes in a story. In the supplied order the CTA is internal and the general headline is late, so the final recruiter item completes the evidence rather than delivering a conventional closing pitch.

file: Library/Posts/60 - Why TF Is Marketing Being Masculinized.md
title: Why TF Is Marketing Being Masculinized
notes:
**The cover uses a joke to make a pattern feel visible right now.** *“You’re seeing it happen in real time”* frames the topic as an unfolding shift, and *“Bros are renaming marketing jobs like they’re applying for NASA”* gives the reader a sharp, specific image. The joke invites agreement before the post asks the reader to consider a larger claim about status and gender.

**Slide 2 acknowledges the obvious objection before making the observation.** *“A job title is just a job title. But the pattern is interesting”* concedes that a title alone may seem trivial, then redirects attention to the repeated association between marketing and *“women’s work.”* The contrast lets the argument move forward without pretending every title change has the same meaning.

**Slide 3 turns the pattern into a change the reader can see.** The list *“technical / AI-heavy / systems-oriented”* follows the earlier list of creativity, aesthetics, emotion, and communication. The closing line, *“All of a sudden, we’re calling everyone an engineer,”* compresses the shift into a dry observation and sets up the historical comparison.

**Slide 4 earns the analogy with a sequence rather than a slogan.** *“Look at programming”* introduces a familiar field, then the slide walks through clerical work, increased profitability, rising prestige, and the rebrand to *“SOFTWARE ENGINEERING.”* Only after that sequence does it name the outcome: *“increasingly male-dominated.”* The order lets the reader infer the parallel before the post returns to marketing.

**Slide 5 explicitly reconnects the history to the present.** *“We’re watching marketing move in a strangely similar direction”* is the hinge, and the list of *“Engineering. Architecture. Systems. Optimization. Infrastructure.”* makes the new technical vocabulary audible. The reader has just seen how a label changed in programming, so this list feels like evidence rather than a detached word bank.

**Slide 6 protects the argument from an easy misreading.** *“And I’m not saying technical skills don’t matter. (They do).”* grants the value of technical competence before asking, *“Why does creative work suddenly feel more legitimate when we give it a technical name?”* The parenthetical keeps the concession brisk; the question points the critique at status, not skill.

**Slide 7 restores the parts of marketing the technical frame left out.** *“words / ideas / stories / psychology”* gives the reader a short inventory, then the line about understanding another human being expands those nouns into a capability. That progression moves from abstract creative inputs to the human outcome the work serves.

**Slide 8 states the thesis only after the history and counterpoint have done their work.** *“We don’t need to make marketing and creativity sound like engineering for it to be taken seriously and be valuable”* is the clearest version of the post’s position. *“Because frankly, it already is to begin with”* gives the long sentence a confident, conversational landing.

**The video closing frame turns the argument into a question that can travel.** *“Why tf is marketing being masculinized?”* strips the preceding explanation down to its most provocative open question. Its placement after the thesis gives it context, while its visual form makes it a memorable ending beat before the promotional slides begin.

**The final three slides shift from argument to creator promotion without changing the voice.** *“Steal my copywriter brain instead”* offers CopyMate as a playful extension of the copywriting theme, then *“Anyway, I’m Sofia”* punctures the inflated mock title before asking for project inquiries. The last *“follow along for more marketing and copywriting”* is a simple account-level close. This is an Argument carousel that appends a promotional and identity coda.

slide_text: You’re seeing it happen in **real time.** Bros are renaming marketing jobs like they’re applying for NASA.

And I know. A job title is just a job title. But the pattern is interesting. Because marketing has historically been associated with things like: Creativity. Aesthetics. Emotion. Communication. And those are things we tend to associate with **women’s work.**
And now **marketing is becoming more:** technical AI-heavy systems-oriented All of a sudden, we’re calling everyone an engineer.

*This isn’t the first time we’ve seen something like this happen.* **Look at programming.** In the 1950s and 60s, programming was largely seen as clerical work. And guess who was doing a lot of it? Women. Then computers became more powerful. The industry became more lucrative. The work became more prestigious. And programming got rebranded as: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING. Over time, the field also became increasingly male-dominated.

We’re watching marketing move in a **strangely similar** **direction.** The more technical marketing becomes, the more we seem to value the technical language around it. Engineering. Architecture. Systems. Optimization. Infrastructure.
And I’m not saying technical skills don’t matter. **(They do).** But here’s the part that makes me pause. **Why does creative work suddenly feel more legitimate when we give it a technical name?**
When marketing, beyond the numbers, is also about: words ideas stories psychology the ability to understand another human being well enough to build a world for them

And that’s a hill I’ll forever die on: **We don’t need to make marketing and creativity sound like engineering for it to be taken seriously and be valuable.** Because frankly, it already is to begin with.

file: Library/Posts/62 - Write the Way You Speak.md
title: Write the Way You Speak
notes:
**The cover opens with a voice instruction, then proves the voice in the same frame.** *“Write the way you speak”* is immediately followed by the contrast between *“this stressed me out SOOOOO bad”* and *“This experience created significant emotional distress.”* The examples make the abstract advice audible before the reader swipes; the deliberately stretched “SOOOOO” is already doing the thing it recommends.

**Slide 2 turns the instruction into a before-and-after the reader can picture.** *“Feeling anxious → Refreshing the tracking link every 6 minutes”* replaces a named feeling with the tiny behavior that reveals it. The previous slide asks the reader to sound like a person; this one shows how a specific, slightly exposing detail makes a person visible.

**Slide 3 changes the scale from word choice to sentence movement.** *“Some thoughts are short. Some pause dramatically. for... wait for it... emotional damage.”* follows the visual examples by explaining the rhythm behind them, then performs that rhythm through the abrupt fragments and intentionally awkward lowercase “for.” The aside *“like what I’m doing now”* lets the slide demonstrate its own point.

**Slide 4 gives the reader small devices for making that voice recognizable.** The list of *“inside jokes, references, reactions, and pauses”* is followed by one example of each, including *“HELLO??? 😭”*. This comes after sentence rhythm because it adds social texture to the voice; the final line names the contrast as writing that feels *“ALIVE”* instead of corporate.

**Slide 5 removes the pressure to get the voice right on the first try.** *“No, really. Write crap. Write bad.”* is a blunt, comic reset after four slides of craft advice. Its short commands enact the looseness being defended, while *“slightly imperfect, oddly specific”* collects the earlier examples into a compact standard for human-sounding lines.

**The sales turn grows out of the problem the carousel has been naming.** Slide 6 says *“If you’re DONE with writing that sounds like it graduated from AI Slop University...”* and introduces Sofia as a copywriter and mentor. The offer to write websites, sales pages, and launch copy follows naturally because the preceding slides have established the desired voice and the reader’s frustration with its opposite; *“DM ME ‘COPY’”* gives that frustration a direct next step.

**The follow prompt offers more of the same voice-led material before the branded loop closes.** *“for more writing and storytelling rabbitholes”* is a relaxed promise rather than a new benefit claim. Slide 8 then supplies *“How to write like a human in the age of AI slop”* as the closing frame video, restating the broader subject after the specific five-point advice and keeping the loop tied to the carousel’s opening idea.

**The carousel is an argument delivered as a short build.** It begins with a claim about natural voice, moves through visual detail, rhythm, and personality, then lowers the stakes with permission to draft badly. The CTA sells help with the exact problem those examples have made concrete, instead of interrupting the teaching with an unrelated pitch.

**Replace vague with visual.** VAGUE | VISUAL Feeling anxious → Refreshing the tracking link every 6 minutes Busy morning → Answering emails with one eye open while downing my second coffee at 7AM Bad date → Realizing halfway that I was carrying the entire conversation on my back Visual writing helps people picture the moment instead of just understanding it logically (and the brain LOVES that!!)

**Mix up your sentence length.** 2 reasons. One, you’re not AI. Two, human conversation naturally changes rhythm. Some thoughts are short. Some pause dramatically. for... wait for it... emotional damage. Some ramble a little because your brain suddenly remembered 14 other stuff halfway through the sentence (like what I’m doing now).

**Add inside jokes, references, reactions, and pauses.** “girl math told me this purchase was basically free” (inside joke) “You can’t sit with us.” (reference IYKYK) “HELLO??? 😭” (reaction) “wait for it…” (pause) These tiny personalities are what make writing feel ALIVE instead of sounding like it was generated in a beige corporate void

**Don’t overthink it.** No, really. Write crap. Write bad. Write things you’ll cringe at later. Some of the best lines ever written sound slightly imperfect, oddly specific, and a little emotionally unhinged… and that’s exactly what makes it human.

file: Library/Posts/63 - Most Brands Look Like This Sheep.md
title: Most Brands Look Like This Sheep
notes:
**The cover makes the branding problem visible before explaining it.** *“Most brands look like this sheep.”* points to an image that is itself made to resemble the familiar flock, so the reader gets a visual joke and a claim at once. The odd specificity of “this sheep” creates a reason to swipe: the next slides will explain what the sheep stands for.

**Slide 2 names the contradiction behind the image.** *“Everyone wants to stand out, but nobody wants to look too different.”* follows the sheep comparison by giving it a human motive. The two halves pull in opposite directions, making conformity feel less like a design accident and more like a choice people make while trying to stay safe.

**Slide 3 shows the outcome of that contradiction.** *“different brands wearing the same colours, fonts & visual language”* turns the abstract wish to fit in into recognizable design ingredients. The repeated sheep now make sense: surface variety can still produce one visual herd.

**Slide 4 shifts from sameness to its consequence.** *“even a good brand can get lost in the herd”* follows the list of shared visual cues by explaining the cost: competent work is not enough when it blends into the category. “Herd” carries the cover image forward, so the metaphor binds the argument rather than decorating it.

**Slide 5 sharpens the diagnosis by separating quality from distinction.** *“The problem isn’t that your branding looks bad. It’s that it looks familiar.”* answers the likely objection that the work is already polished. That clarification follows the consequence on slide 4 and makes the real issue harder to dismiss: the brand may look good and still be forgettable.

**Slide 6 states the practical test in one sentence.** *“Your brand should be recognisable before anyone has to read the name.”* gives a positive standard after the previous slides have defined what fails. It moves the reader from noticing visual sameness to imagining a brand whose identity is legible without its label.

**Slide 7 makes the solution a category-level ambition.** *“It’s about making the category.”* completes the contrast with *“fitting into the category”* from the same slide. This is the argument’s biggest step: once recognition is the test, distinctiveness can shape what customers expect from the whole space.

**The CTA keeps the sheep metaphor alive while making a clear offer.** *“Break the bhe[d] cha[a]l.”* is a visual wordplay on “herd” and the flock imagery; *“Build a brand that looks like nobody else”* translates the joke into a service promise. The closing line *“Branding that refuses to follow the herd”* echoes slide 4, giving the final frame a memorable phrase that belongs to this specific argument.

**This is an argument carousel with a visual metaphor doing structural work.** The sheep begins as a joke, reappears as the consequence of sameness, and returns in the CTA as the thing the brand can escape. Each slide advances the claim from shared desire, to shared style, to lost recognition, and finally to category-making.

notes:
**The cover sells professional opportunity in the language of internet luck.** "LinkedIn can make you / the luckiest girl / on the internet" attacks the assumption that LinkedIn belongs to a stiff professional identity separate from the reader's social life. "Can make you" makes the platform an agent of transformation, while "luckiest girl" supplies an identity more attractive than "effective networker." "many of us spent years avoiding LinkedIn" includes the writer in that avoidance, so "but that’s changing" does not sound like scolding. "posting selfies," "telling personal stories" and "sharing opinions" make the unfamiliar platform legible through behaviours the reader already knows.

**The “hybrid” is the main insight, and its two halves answer different desires.** "entertainment platform like Instagram" plus "referral network you usually only get from someone personally recommending you" lands on slide 2. The first half promises familiar expression; the second adds scarce professional access. That pairing explains why the cover's luck might be more than optimism: public content can take on the function of a private introduction. Slide 4 later expands this exact mechanism rather than introducing a different benefit.

**The question arrives as a closing challenge before the supplied sequence has finished arguing.** "so... what are you waiting for?" is on slide 3, followed by "let’s make LinkedIn your new favourite place to post." There is no unfolding chain of questions; this single question presumes the permission and hybrid argument have already removed the objection. "let’s" immediately replaces the challenge with companionship. In these images the CTA comes before the newsfeed, audience and workload explanations, so its immediate earning is limited to what slides 1–2 have supplied.

**“LUCKY GIRL” lets the reader request the offer in the identity the cover promised.** "comment LUCKY GIRL" leads directly to "Lucky Girl LinkedIn coaching cohort." The keyword, aspiration and product name all belong to the same vocabulary, so the response does not require changing from a social mood into a technical purchase discussion. "I’ll send you the details" makes the next step information rather than enrolment, while "to start posting" attaches the cohort to the first behaviour the argument wants.

**Slide 4 turns a platform feature into a sentence the reader wants said about them.** "they have commented on or liked" explains distribution, then "you were a brilliant speaker! / can’t wait to work with you again" supplies its human consequence. The concluding "not only makes you look great ... but also puts you ... in front of their entire network" expands praise into access. "lovely comment" keeps the mechanism socially warm; "someone senior at the right company" makes the imagined benefit professionally precise.

**The audience claim narrows into four recognisable uses instead of remaining a huge number.** "over 134M people" is paired with "97% of them ... just scrolling," then interpreted as "a pretty captive audience." The examples move through "influencers," "creatives," "founders" and "creators," each tied to a different outcome: strategic thinking, opportunities, loyal followers or collaborations. "LinkedIn demands less of people" moves the benefit from professional access to personal relief. The last contrast, "four hours" versus "fifteen minutes," makes a failed attempt affordable; the rhythm ends on the smaller loss rather than another promise of success. This is an **Argument / invitation**: permission, a referral mechanism and manageable effort support a coaching offer, with the invitation appearing mid-sequence in the supplied order.

title: How to Be Obscenely Consistent
notes:
**The cover promises consistency, then quietly loosens its usual definition.** *“How to Be Obscenely Consistent. EVEN IF YOU’VE FALLEN OFF BEFORE.”* The first line sounds like a familiar discipline pitch; the subtitle addresses people who have already broken their streak, so the tension is whether consistency can include interruption.

**Slide 2 turns a common setback into the argument’s target.** *“I think we made consistency WAY too dependent on never f*cking up.”* The examples of three missed days and two missed weeks make the all-or-nothing rule feel recognizable before the sharper ending says the interruption may not be the main issue. It redirects blame without yet giving a solution.

**Slide 3 supplies a compact counterexample instead of a lecture.** *“They just... make the next thing.”* The people described as consistent still disappear, so the distinction is their return ritual, not perfect attendance. Its short, plain phrase lands after the elaborate planner and Monday-reset scenarios, making the behavior feel almost embarrassingly simple.

**Slide 4 makes the cost of perfection personal and measurable.** *“Two posts existed. Zero would have been objectively worse.”* The five-versus-two plan gives the self-judgment a concrete object, then exposes the absurd comparison with zero. The admission about ADHD lets the reader see the mechanism at work rather than receive generic encouragement.

**Slide 5 changes the unit of success from the ideal week to the available week.** *“If the normal week has room for five posts and this week only has room for two... then maybe we post two.”* “Wild, I know” carries the speaker’s old resistance into the reader’s likely reaction; the next sentence shows how rejecting a smaller version can turn five impossible posts into none.

**Slides 6–7 locate the practical friction in rebuilding after a gap.** *“Some parts of your process should survive a crap week without you”* names a system that can hold templates, ideas, and recurring conversations; the following questions test whether those pieces are ready when she returns. The jokes about “Wednesday Tinna” and becoming “fascinating on command” keep the operational point rooted in an actual week.

**Slides 8–9 finish the redefinition before naming the product.** *“whether the thing still knows what to do AFTER I stop”* becomes the standard, and *“there should just be a lot less to rebuild”* turns that standard into a clear diagnosis. The cause-and-effect chain makes the system feel like a response to the problem already demonstrated, not a sudden sales detour.

**The CTA earns its offer by echoing the mechanism the carousel has built.** *“build the repeatable parts once and then keep pulling from them”* answers the repeated return-to-zero problem, while the comment keyword gives a specific next action. The genre is **Argument / Build**: it challenges a rigid belief about consistency, then points toward a repeatable content process.

slide_text: **How to Be Obscenely Consistent.** *EVEN IF YOU’VE FALLEN OFF BEFORE.*

**I think we made consistency WAY too dependent on never f*cking up.** Miss three days and suddenly we need a comeback plan. Miss two weeks and apparently we are “completely starting from scratch”. Mate, why? Your life interrupted you, and it is probably going to do that again. If every interruption sends the whole thing back to zero, **I’m starting to think the interruption is not actually the main issue.**

**The people I think are ridiculously consistent still disappear sometimes.** They just don’t turn returning into a ceremonial event. No new planner, “I’ll do it on Monday” and most definitely no “this month I’m finally going to be disciplined”. **They just... make the next thing.** Which sounds annoyingly simple until you realise how much energy we waste waiting to feel properly BACK.

**I used to be terrible at this.** If I planned five posts and managed two, somehow my ADHD brain did not register TWO POSTS. It registered... she failed the plan. Which makes absolutely no sense. Two posts existed. **Zero would have been objectively worse.** But zero came with the very attractive fantasy that next week I would execute everything perfectly, apparently as a completely different woman.

**And yes, sometimes the plan needs to get smaller.** This one took me embarrassingly long. If the normal week has room for five posts and this week only has room for two... **then maybe we post two.** Wild, I know. For a long time I treated the smaller version like it somehow didn’t count, which is how five impossible posts became zero surprisingly often.

**Some parts of your process should survive a crap week without you.** I want the template to still exist. I want my ideas to still be sitting somewhere instead of relying on me remembering the brilliant thought I had while driving three days ago. And I want to know the handful of conversations I can always come back to without Wednesday Tinna having to rebuild the entire content department because Monday and Tuesday went non verbal. **That poor woman has enough going on.**

**Now I care a lot more about what happens when I come back.** Do I roughly know what I’m posting, or am I opening Instagram and starting the whole decision-making process again? Have I already decided the formats? Is there somewhere to pull an idea from, or am I meant to become fascinating on command after a week where everything went to sh*t? Because THAT is usually the bit that **makes returning feel heavier than it needs to.**

**Maybe consistency is less about never stopping than we make it out to be.** I’m much more interested now in whether the thing still knows what to do AFTER I stop. **Because I will. You will.** Something unexpected is bound to happen. I’d rather build around that reality than keep designing a plan for a woman who apparently never gets tired, distracted, sick or interrupted. That woman is probably doing 5am cold plunges and journaling straight after in a parallel reality.

**So if you keep “falling off”, I’d look at what you are actually coming back TO.** Because if every return means deciding the formats again, finding ideas again, figuring out what the hell you even talk about again and somehow matching all of that to whatever capacity you have left that week... of course coming back feels heavy. I don’t think the answer is getting better at forcing yourself through that. I think **there should just be a lot less to rebuild.**

**That is basically the whole reason I built The Content Engine.** I wanted a system where I already knew what I talk about, where ideas come from, which formats I can actually sustain and what each piece of content is meant to do for the business. So instead of starting from scratch every Monday, you build the repeatable parts once and then keep pulling from them. If you want a content system you can actually keep using when life gets messy, **comment “MELON” and I’ll send you the details.**

**The cover sells a paradox, then slide 2 states the governing principle.** *“How Minimalist Design Takes More Work”* reverses the assumption that less content means less effort; *“Less on the canvas means more pressure on every choice”* makes that reversal concrete. **The numbered middle gives the argument a clear inventory shape.** *“There's Nowhere to Hide”* opens with exposed flaws, then later points move through purposeful elements, typography, positioning, and restraint. Follow for more practical graphic design insights and creative thinking frameworks.”* The CTA is earned by showing the account's practical framework first; the genre is **Inventory / Argument**, a numbered set of design principles supporting the claim that minimalism demands more work.

title: How Pleasure Attracts Luck
notes:
**The hook makes an unexpected causal claim: “HOW PLEASURE ATTRACTS LUCK.”** “Pleasure” and “luck” are usually treated as separate things, so putting them together creates an argument the reader wants to see proved. The short cover leaves the mechanism open, and slide 2 begins supplying it immediately.

**Slide 2 narrows the claim into something observable: “YOUR STATE CHANGES WHAT YOU NOTICE.”** Rather than promise that pleasure magically summons opportunities, the carousel says attention shifts with tension and relaxation. That grounded mechanism gives the big cover claim a plausible first rung.

**Slide 3 names the opposing state: “SURVIVAL MODE MAKES YOUR WORLD SMALLER.”** The sentence “Not because possibility disappears” anticipates a possible misreading, then explains how threat scanning makes possibilities harder to see. The movement from contraction to “what could be different” turns a familiar anxiety response into the obstacle in the argument.

**The fourth slide pivots from limitation to recognition with “LUCK NEEDS YOU TO NOTICE IT.”** Its list—“An introduction. An idea. An invitation.”—gives luck tangible forms after two slides about attention. The closing image of a door missed while preparing for what could go wrong makes the mechanism easy to picture.

**The middle develops two consequences in sequence: “WHEN YOU FEEL GOOD, YOU MOVE DIFFERENTLY” and “PEOPLE FEEL THE DIFFERENCE TOO.”** Slide 5 turns inner state into tiny actions; slide 6 turns those actions into better connection and unplanned opportunities. The repeated “You… differently” gives the claim a spoken rhythm while keeping the progression clear: self, then others.

**“SOMETIMES ‘LUCK’ IS JUST YOU BEING AVAILABLE” gives the argument its reframe.** “You noticed the opening. You trusted the invitation. You started the conversation. file: Library/Posts/70 - Why Does Everything Look the Same.md
title: Why Does Everything Look the Same
notes:
**The cover turns a common observation into a question.** “Why Does Everything Look the Same?” asks the reader to inspect a pattern they may already have noticed across restaurants, shops, and brands. Its breadth creates recognition first, while the fragmented portrait and stark red field add urgency without answering the question.

**Slide 2 makes the complaint concrete before naming its cause.** “Walk into a trendy taquería, coffee shop, restaurant or hotel...” supplies familiar places, then “Bold type. Retro references. Hand-drawn details.” gives the sameness a visible vocabulary. The short list lets readers mentally recognize the style before the next slide explains how it spreads.

**The question chain moves from copying to choosing.** Slide 4 contrasts “What is everyone doing?” with “What makes sense for us?” and slide 6 expands that into three tests: personality, recognizability, and standing apart. The sequence replaces an external reference point with questions about fit, so the advice feels like a decision process rather than a ban on trends.

**The key insight is a distinction between relevance and recognition.** “Relevant ≠ Recognizable” reframes the problem: a brand can look current while remaining forgettable. Slide 5’s closing line, “It looks like itself,” supplies the positive standard, and slide 7 makes it usable through the metaphor “Use Trends as Ingredients, Not the Entire Recipe.”

**The diction builds its argument through paired opposites.** “Current” and “memorable,” “stand apart” and “blend in,” then “relevant” and “recognizable” give the carousel a steady contrast rhythm. The sequence moves from naming the sameness, to diagnosing trend dependence, to giving the reader a simple test for making choices.

**The brand examples support the point without interrupting it.** The visible wordmarks VICIO, BRUSC, rhode, and LOEWE sit beside distinct visual references, while the text insists that a point of view is what makes current cues recognizable. That visual evidence helps the reader see the distinction between using a trend and letting it define the whole identity.

**The CTA follows the subject’s natural next step.** “Join our newsletter” offers more thoughts on branding, marketing, and strategy, which is a direct continuation of the carousel’s argument. It is a clear subscription invitation, though the post does not give a specific promised issue or resource; the reader is asked to continue following the same point of view.

**This is an Argument.** It opens with a cultural complaint, identifies trend dependence as the mechanism, reframes the standard from relevance to recognizability, and closes with a newsletter invitation. The question-and-contrast chain carries the reader from recognition to a principle they can apply to their own brand.

slide_text: LEONORA ESTUDIO **Why Does Everything Look the Same?**

Walk into a trendy taquería, coffee shop, restaurant or hotel... and chances are, you’ve seen the visual language before. Bold type. Retro references. Hand-drawn details. A very specific kind of “cool.”

**The Pinterest Effect** We have more visual inspiration than ever. Pinterest. Instagram. TikTok. Behance. Moodboards. We see what’s working, save what we like, and slowly start speaking the same visual language.

**Trends Aren’t the Problem.** **Trend dependency is.** When the trend becomes the starting point instead of the brand, everything starts to look interchangeable. The question isn't: *What is everyone doing?* It’s: *What makes sense for us?*

**Relevant ≠ Recognizable** A trend can make your brand feel current. But current doesn’t always mean memorable. You can follow all the right cues and still look like everyone else. BECAUSE A MEMORABLE BRAND DOESN’T JUST LOOK GOOD... **It looks like itself.**

BEFORE FOLLOWING A TREND, ASK: Does it fit our personality? Does it make us more recognizable? Does it help us stand apart — or blend in? **The goal isn't to avoid trends.** **It’s to know how to use them.**

**Use Trends as Ingredients,** **Not the Entire Recipe** The brands we remember aren’t necessarily the ones that never follow trends. They’re the ones that know who they are first. They filter what’s happening around them through their own point of view.
**Being relevant is great.** **Being recognizable is better.** Build a brand that feels current without feeling interchangeable. That’s where having a point of view makes all the difference.

file: Library/Posts/71 - The Art of Taking Nothing Personally.md
title: The Art of Taking Nothing Personally
notes:
**The cover promises relief from a familiar reflex.** “The Art of Taking Nothing Personally” names the emotional skill, while “remember that you cannot control how others behave, only how you respond...” states its central principle in plain language. The subtitle narrows the title’s broad idea into a problem many readers recognize: other people’s behavior feels outside their control.

**The numbered advice begins by making difference ordinary.** “Everyone Thinks Differently” starts with varying beliefs, moods, and perspectives, then asks readers not to expect identical reactions. This lowers the temperature of disagreement before the later advice tackles rejection and rude behavior.

**The advice pages repeatedly turn attention back toward choice.** “Not every comment needs a reaction” and “So avoid carrying emotions that were created by someone else's problems” shift the reader’s focus from judging other people to choosing what to attend to. The short standalone statements create a calm, aphoristic pace that suits the topic.

**The sequence jumps among numbered points rather than developing them in order.** After “1. Everyone Thinks Differently,” the carousel moves to “4. Learn to Let Go of Small Things,” then “6. Focus on Your Own Peace of Mind,” “5. Accept That Rejection Happens,” and “2. Remember That Other People's Behavior Is About Them.” The advice stays on-theme, but the skipped numbering can make the accumulation feel loosely assembled instead of like a deliberate progression.

**The two quotations interrupt the advice with broader statements.** “Real life begins... when you stop living your life based on what others think of you” appears between principles 2 and 3, while the Paulo Coelho quote closes the sequence. Both echo the theme of emotional independence, but the first arrives without attribution and the closing quote shifts the final beat from the author’s advice to a borrowed maxim.

**The book promotion grows directly out of the reader’s stated pain.** “If you overthink what people say, take things to heart, or care too much about others’ opinion...” identifies the target reader before promising help with taking nothing personally. The “link in bio” instruction makes the action clear; a following product image keeps the book present before the final quotation.

**This is an Inventory / Argument with a promotional ending.** Numbered lessons supply a set of reasons to detach from others’ behavior, and the opening title binds them to one central belief: focus on your response. The book offer is tied to that belief, although the sequence of lesson numbers and the last quotation give the carousel a collage-like finish rather than a final summary of the argument.

file: Library/Posts/72 - Perfect Looks Fake Now.md
title: Perfect Looks Fake Now
notes:
**The cover is four words and a reversal of a compliment.** "Perfect / looks fake / now" takes the word every creator is working towards and makes it the accusation. "Now" is the word doing the work: it says this was not true before, which is exactly what slide 2 goes back to explain.

**Slides 2 and 3 build the old rule before breaking it.** "For years, polish meant trust" and "Perfect used to signal: quality / taste / effort / professionalism" spend two slides making the reader agree with the thing about to be taken away. The past tense ("meant", "used to") keeps the tension open across both slides without a question being asked.

**The turn is one line and one piece of evidence.** "Then AI made perfect cheap." The screenshot under it is a real artist having to defend hand-made work as not AI. The argument is not asserted, it is shown happening to someone, and "People can't tell anymore what's authentic" names what the reader just watched.

**Slide 5 gives the mechanism in plain cause and effect.** "And when perfect gets easier to make, it stops feeling special." This is the sentence the whole post rests on, and it arrives only after the evidence.

**"Too smooth. too clean. too generated." is three in a row where the last one costs.** The first two are things people used to want. The third reveals what they now mean.

**The answer is split over three slides.** "So what stands out now isn't perfection." / "It's presence." / the four examples. The negative gets its own slide, the one-word answer gets its own slide, and only then is it made concrete ("A real opinion. A weird detail. A lived story. A human point of view."). Each slide ends with the reader needing the next.

**The close swaps one word in a question.** "Don't ask: How do I make this look perfect?" then "Ask: How do I make this feel human?" Same sentence, "look perfect" against "feel human". It hands the reader a replacement habit without a list of steps.

**The CTA is a question, not an offer.** "What makes content feel human to you? Tell me in the comments." No keyword, no freebie. It reuses "feel human" from the slide before, so the ask is the reader answering the question they were just told to ask themselves.

**Twelve slides, none over about fifteen words.** Same build as [[38 - Stop Sharing How Much Money You Make Online]] by the same account: one thought per slide, serif statement plus a handwritten aside, an Argument with no method.

For years, polish *meant* trust. Clean visuals. Good lighting. Perfect copy.
Perfect used to signal: quality taste effort professionalism
Then AI made perfect cheap. People can't tell anymore what's authentic.
And when *perfect* gets easier to make, it stops feeling special.
Now perfect *can* feel... too smooth. too clean. too generated.
So what stands out now isn't *perfection*.
It's *presence*.
A real opinion. A weird detail. A lived story. A human point of view.
Don't ask: "How do I make this *look* perfect?"
Ask: "How do I make this *feel* human?"
What makes content *feel* human to you? Tell me in the comments.

file: Library/Posts/73 - 3 Levels of Branding.md
title: 3 Levels of Branding
notes:
**The cover names a ladder and then tells the reader they are on the bottom rung.** "3 Levels of Branding" is a plain named model. "Most brands never get past Level 1" is the line that makes it personal: nobody reads that and assumes they are the exception, so they swipe to check.

**Slide 2 turns the model into a self-test before explaining anything.** "Which level you're operating at?" The levels are labelled on the chess pieces but not defined. The reader now has a question about themselves that only the next ten slides can answer.

**Each level gets the same two-slide card.** A name slide ("Level 1: Random Pairing", with what it is) followed by a detail slide ("What Level 1 Looks Like", "How to Get to Level 2", "The Level 3 Flywheel"). The repeat lets the reader predict the shape and read faster, and every heading is a label that makes sense alone.

**Level 1 is described so the reader recognises themselves.** "Posting without a plan / Showing up when you feel like it / Your audience can't explain what you do in one sentence", then "If someone heard your name tomorrow, they'd have nothing to say about you." The list is behaviour, the closing line is the cost. "96%" tells them they are in the majority, which makes it safe to admit.

**The examples are brands everyone already holds an association for.** "Nike → athletic greatness", "Harley-Davidson → freedom & adventure". The reader proves the idea to themselves because the association fires before they finish reading the line. "They didn't stumble into those associations. They chose them." is the X, not Y that makes it a method.

**"The Part Most People Skip" is an info gap in a heading.** It promises something the reader has missed, then delivers a reversal: "It's about what you refuse to pair yourself with."

**The Level 2 to Level 3 difference is one swapped phrase.** "They associate you with success stories." against "They associate you with their own success." Two short lines, three words apart, carrying the whole top of the model.

**The post recaps itself twice before the ask.** "Why Most Brands Stay Stuck" restates the levels as failure points, and "The Framework" restates them as one diagram with "Skip one and the whole thing collapses." For an abstract model this is the wrap-up that ties the items together and gives the reader a slide worth saving (every slide carries "Save for later").

**The CTA qualifies instead of giving.** "Looking to build a Level 3 personal brand? Comment "Level" and let's see if we're a good fit." The comment word comes from the post's own vocabulary, and the offer is a conversation about working together, not a freebie. The line before it, "Your brand already exists whether you define it or not", removes the option of doing nothing.

**Heavier slides than most of the file.** Roughly 30 to 60 words a slide with a heading on every body slide, bullets or numbered cards on most, and a diagram on two. A model post where the design carries structure that short-line argument posts carry with pacing. Compare [[61 - 5 of These AI Agents Are a Waste of Money]] for the repeated card, and [[72 - Perfect Looks Fake Now]] for the opposite build.

Every brand sits at one of three levels. The gap between forgettable and worth fighting for? Which level you're operating at? *Footer on every slide 2–12:* Save for later · Swipe →

Level 1: **Random Pairing** This is where 96% of brands live. — Posting without a plan — Showing up when you feel like it — Your audience can't explain what you do in one sentence *A bishop breaking apart.*

**What Level 1 Looks Like** 01 Content with no recurring theme 02 Visuals that don't match the message 03 Collaborating with anyone who'll have you If someone heard your name tomorrow, they'd have nothing to say about you.

Level 2: **Intentional Pairing** You pick the associations you want attached to your name. Then you pair yourself with those things on purpose. Nike → athletic greatness Harley-Davidson → freedom & adventure They didn't stumble into those associations. They chose them. *A stone knight.*
**How to Get to Level 2** Three questions. Work backwards from here: What do I want to be known for? What do I have to do to earn that? What do I need to learn to pull it off?

**The Part Most People Skip** Level 2 isn't only about what you pair yourself with. It's about what you refuse to pair yourself with. If you keep showing up alongside people your audience doesn't trust, that association sticks to you. *A knight crumbling.*

Level 3: **Audience Ownership** This is where everything changes. Level 2 They associate you with success stories. Level 3 They associate you with *their own* success. Now they believe anything they invest in you pays back more than they put in. *A stone queen.*

**The Level 3 Flywheel** This is where everything changes. Share lessons + frameworks (free) → Audience trusts you (built through proof) → They take action and get results → They associate you with their wins → *(back to the start)* When you finally make an offer, the conversation isn't "convince me." It's "take my money."

**Why Most Brands Stay Stuck** Level 1 brands Post without intention. Level 2 brands Pair intentionally, but never build enough trust to reach Level 3. And the ones who try to skip straight to monetization without earning trust? You can't shortcut your way from forgettable to unforgettable.

**The Framework** Level 1 — Random pairing. Unclear positioning. Inconsistent output. Audience doesn't stick around. ↓ Level 2 — Intentional pairing. Clear associations. Consistent execution. Trust starts building. ↓ Level 3 — Audience ownership. Your audience wins because of you. Trust becomes the product. Each level builds on the one before it. Skip one and the whole thing collapses.

Your brand already exists whether you define it or not. The only question is which level you're building at. Looking to build a Level 3 personal brand? Comment **"Level"** and let's see if we're a good fit.

I started by giving it everything. Now, I know there are 3rd party tools that you can use to connect your Instagram to Claude, however, I have tried a few and they have not been able to connect properly. (If you know of a good tool, comment below please!) So, for now, I screenshotted allll my analytics. 90 days of insights. My top 10 posts. The posts that got me the most followers. All the big flops. My bio. My follower count. My actual goal. etc. etc. etc.

Then we argued about my pillars for 30 minutes. Not "what should I post." That question gets you generic answers. I told it what I'm building, who I want in this audience, and what I actually care about. Then we went back and forth until the pillars were right. What we landed on: Building in public — the majority. The wins, the flops, the doubt. This is the account. Thrifting & fashion — my reach engine. It brings in people who have never heard of me. Travel — the smallest, and the most useful for brand partnerships.

But every pillar had to tie back to Harvi. Otherwise it's just a personal account with good analytics. Harvi is about finding your people in a city where you don't know anyone. So: Thrifting — the vintage community is one of the strongest, most tight-knit communities there is. Every store I post is a real place where people who love the same thing already gather. That's Harvi. Travel — arriving somewhere and knowing nobody is literally the reason Harvi exists.

Then I told it exactly what I wanted. Not "give me content ideas." That gets you a never ending list with no strategy. I said (shortened version. I'll DM you the full prompt if you comment "claude"): "You are the world's greatest social media strategist. I want to hit 10,000 followers in one week. Here are all of my analytics. Go through them, tell me what is actually working and what isn't, and then tell me exactly what to post and why." The role play wasn't the trick. Giving it a real number, a real deadline, and real data was. I would imagine most people ask for ideas. Ask it to look at your actual numbers first and the ideas come out completely different.

Then it told me what was actually broken. And it was not what I thought. 328,000 people saw my content in 30 days. Only 0.13% of them followed me.... Healthy is somewhere between 0.4% and 0.8%. So I did not have a reach problem. I had a "nobody who sees this knows why they should stay" problem.

The first fix was my bio, and it took 4 minutes. My name field just said "Jessi Anderson." That field is searchable, and I was using it for nothing. Now it says Jessi Anderson | Building in Public. People searching that phrase can find me now. That is free discovery I was leaving on the table. Then the bio itself. All I said was "Co-founder of Harvi" Now line one says what I'm building. Line two says what I'm documenting. Line three is the thrifting and travel, in my actual voice. Smallest change of the whole week.

Then for the Claude magic... It suggested the very first post to create to get to the 10K mark in a week... And let me just tell ya, that one post got me close to 100K views and 400 followers.... So, what was already an aggressive 5 day goal, I hit in one day with one post...

But even more important than 10K. 0.13% to 0.83%. That is the percentage of people who see my content and actually follow me. It went up more than 6x in one day. This number is the #1 most important thing to every single thing I post from now on.

Now that same chat tracks everything. I screenshot my analytics and drop them in, sometimes twice a day. What's working, what's flopping, what to do next. It already knows my voice, my pillars, and every number from the last month, so I never have to explain myself again.

The goal is now 20K in two months. It's an insanely aggressive number, but I shall document the whole thing so we can see how it goes together. Here's what I actually learned from this week though. None of it worked because of just a prompt. - It worked because five vintage stores shared my post. - Because my friend Clint told me to pin a comment to each post about who I am/what I am building - Because I learned how to think about community at Entreprenista - Because 2,409 people took the time to comment and I took the time to answer every one on that post A personal brand isn't an audience you collect. It's the people who show up for you and the people you show up for. That's the whole thing I'm building at Harvi, by the way.

10. GET A **SECOND OPINION** *two models catch what one misses* - let a second model attack your code - tell it to think like a hacker - point it at payments and API keys

**The Biggest Distractions Don't Look Dangerous.** The biggest threats to your future rarely look harmful. Endless *scrolling, entertainment, and constant notifications* don't feel dangerous, but they quietly steal the one resource you can never get back your **attention**. **Protect your focus** before temptation appears, because prevention is easier than recovery.

*#2 The Cyclops* **Ego Can Create Bigger Problems Than the Obstacle Itself.** Winning isn't enough knowing when to stay **silent** matters too. Many people damage their own progress by **seeking recognition too early**, proving themselves unnecessarily, or letting success inflate their ego. Humility often protects what pride puts at risk.

*#3 Calypso* **Not Every Beautiful Place is Meant for You** Many people settle for a life that feels **comfortable** but lacks meaning. Don't confuse **convenience with fulfillment.** The easier path isn't always the one that leads to the life you truly want.

*#4 Circe* **Your Habits Slowly Shape Your Identity.** Every **habit** is shaping your identity. - The books you read - The people you spend time with - The content you consume All *influence* the person you'll become years from now. The things you repeatedly *consume* slowly change who you become.

*#5 The Lotus-Eaters* **Comfort can quietly steal your future.** You don't always fail because life becomes difficult. Sometimes you fail because **life becomes comfortable** enough that you stop growing. Never become so comfortable that you *forget* the future you're trying to build.

*#6 Helios' Sacred Cattle* **One Moment of Temptation Can Cost Everything** Most regrets begin with the thought, *"Just this once."* Self-control matters most when **temptation** feels completely justified. **Small decisions** often shape your biggest outcomes.

*#7 Scylla* **Sometimes The Perfect Choice Doesn't Exist.** Life often gives you **difficult choices** instead of perfect ones. Waiting for the *ideal* solution can leave you stuck. **Progress comes from choosing** the option that protects your future, even if it's imperfect.

**The Real Monsters** The Odyssey isn't really about defeating mythical creatures. It's about defeating the *monsters* within **yourself**: - Distraction. - Comfort. - Ego. - Impatience. - Poor decisions. Thousands of years later, those monsters still exist. They've simply changed their ***appearance***.

slide_text: How to sell *ANYTHING* to *ANYONE*

1. Earn belief before the pitch *WHAT:* people size you up before they size up your offer. *WHY:* trust removes risk. we say yes to who we believe. *HOW:* 1) give value first. 2) match their energy, don't perform. *EXAMPLE:* the one who helps even when there's nothing to gain.

2. Sell what changes, not what you're holding *WHAT:* they're buying a better version of their life, not the item. *WHY:* we act on the picture we imagine, not the specs. *HOW:* 1) finish "so you can \_\_\_". 2) describe their after, in their words. *EXAMPLE:* not "a gym plan", "fitting your old jeans again."

3. Your ears close more deals than your mouth *their words are the whole pitch* *WHAT:* you can't fix what you never let them explain. *WHY:* people trust a fix built from their own words, not a script. *HOW:* 1) ask, then stay quiet. 2) repeat their problem back first. *EXAMPLE:* the doctor who asks before they prescribe.

4. Hand them the idea, not the verdict *let it feel like their discovery* *WHAT:* the strongest yes is the one they think they found alone. *WHY:* we defend our own conclusions, resist someone else's. *HOW:* 1) offer choices, not orders. 2) ask questions that lead there. *EXAMPLE:* "most people go with x, but it's your call."

5. Shrink the downside what: the real objection is fear of getting it wrong. how: cut it with guarantees, trials, small steps, proof. 6. Ease outsells force what: pressure breeds resistance, calm breeds trust. how: leave them an exit. it's what makes yes feel safe.

You're not pushing a product. you're clearing the way for a yes. earn belief. sell the after. listen first. hand them the idea. shrink the risk. ease off. master this and you can sell anything. Save this and Follow for more

slide_text: How to raise your rates ✱ Without losing clients
If you're stuck at ₹30k/month as a social media manager and you know you're worth more. *Here's exactly how to do it:*

STEP 1: AUDIT YOUR CLIENTS Divide your existing clients into 3 groups: - **Dream clients** (pay well, easy to work with, results-driven) - **Good clients** (decent, no drama, moderate pay) - **Problem clients** (always asking for discounts, difficult, low pay)

STEP 3: DECIDE YOUR NEW RATE What's your new rate? Calculate: - Your time spent per client - Results you deliver - Market rate for your experience - What feels good AND sustainable Don't jump ₹30k → ₹100k. Go ₹30k → ₹50k → ₹75k.

STEP 4: WHAT TO SAY TO EXISTING CLIENTS Refer to this script (3 months before increase): "Hey [name], I've loved working with you. Your account has grown [X%] and we've built solid systems together. Starting [date], my rates are increasing to ₹50k/month to reflect the value I'm delivering. Your current rate stays ₹30k through [date] as a thank you for being an amazing client. After that, we can either continue at the new rate or I can help transition you to another manager. Let me know your thoughts."

You might lose 1-2 problem clients. Good. You'll gain new clients at higher rates. Better. Your existing dream clients will stay. Best. And your net result: Same number of clients. 50%+ more revenue. You're not losing money. You're exchanging low-value clients for high-value ones. Your brain will fight this at first. And that's normal.

before anything, understand this... the ad doesn't start with the product. because you aren't selling features. you aren't even selling benefits. you are selling the emotional outcome customers believe the product gives them. if you don't know the emotion you are selling, the ad has no direction.

this is where the map of consciousness comes in... *Chart:* Map of Consciousness, Developed By David R. Hawkins (levels from Shame 20 up to Enlightenment 700-1000) it's a framework from dr. david hawkins that basically shows how different emotional states calibrate at different levels.
lower consciousness = stuck, powerless. higher consciousness = open, willing to act. your customer is already sitting somewhere on that map. your job is to know where they are.

so how does this translate into marketing? most buyers are sitting in a lower state around the problem you solve. they feel stuck. frustrated. ashamed. apathetic. your copy's job is to move them from lower consciousness to higher consciousness and then BACK to lower consciousness Bringin them back down is where the money is made...
because pain hits harder after someone gets a taste of the better reality. that is an emotional delta *Hand-drawn curve:* 1 Guilt → 2 Courage → 3 Guilt, with "Emotional Delta" marked on the drop.

think about it like this... someone who grew up poor and stayed poor knows pain. but someone who grew up poor, got rich, tasted what life feels like with money, and then lost it all. that's a different type of pain. because now they know what they lost. your copy needs to create the same emotional contrast.

but you can't create contrast from guesses. you need to know where your customer is before you try to move them. what they feel, believe, blame, are ashamed of, and what they secretly want instead. that is why research comes before copy.

the good part is, most of this research can be done with AI. but only if you feed it the right process. If you want my process for researching your customers so you know them better than they know themselves. dm me "FOUNDATION" and I'll send it to you for free.

file: Library/Posts/99 - You're Only 100 LinkedIn Posts Away.md
title: You're Only 100 LinkedIn Posts Away
notes:
**The cover is a countable promise.** "You're only 100 LinkedIn posts away" turns a vague goal (become a thought leader) into a task with a number. Slide 2 repeats the phrase four times with a different prize each time, so the benefits arrive as a list with one rhythm.

**The objection is "this sounds crazy" and the answer is arithmetic.** Slide 3 gives two numbers (1 billion users, under 2% posting weekly) and one consequence (post once a week and you are in the top 2%). "And those billion people? They're the same people competing for your next job." turns the statistic into stakes.

**The real barrier is renamed.** "Cringe" is the author's word for what stops people. Slide 4 says it outright: "The cringe is the barrier. Not the action." Slide 5 draws it as a mountain with the reader on the slope. Naming the feeling lets the reader admit it, and it is the hook for the program, which "addresses cringe first".

**The sale is told as a personal circumstance.** "Buuuut here's the thing: I'm about to go on maternity leave." The reason for the offer is real and specific, so the price drop ($5,000 to $850) reads as a one-time event, not a discount. The "50 people" limit and "Once they're gone, they're gone" close it. Compare [[84 - How to Sell Anything to Anyone]] for the sales method the post follows.
